Event title: Next-generation biodiversity analytics: BON in a Box tapping into Earth Observation intelligence
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
Email addresses of contacts: samara.manzin@mcgill.ca, jean-michel.lord@mcgill.ca, nina.obiar@mcgill.ca, guillaume.larocque@mcgill.ca, marc.paganini@esa.int, federica.marando@esa.int
List any other organizations, collaborat: European Space Agency (ESA)
Event description:
Earth Observation (EO) data holds enormous potential for biodiversity monitoring, but remains difficult to integrate directly into biodiversity workflows or indicator calculations. This session presents a collaboration between the European Space Agency (ESA) and GEO BON that addresses this gap through interoperability rather than duplication of effort.
The session will show how interoperability between ESA's openEO interface and GEO BON's BON in a Box combines the strengths of both platforms: cloud-based EO data processing with biodiversity workflows. Through a demonstration, presenters will show how Earth Observation data can be integrated into workflows to enhance biodiversity monitoring and indicator reporting.
Presenters will explore how this complementarity can make EO data more usable for biodiversity monitoring, and how continued ESA–GEO BON collaboration can strengthen the pipeline from raw observations to decision-ready indicators, in support of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Discussion will center on the capacity and skill gaps countries face in putting EO data to practical use, and how this integration, and future ones, can help address these barriers.

Event title: Implementing data sovereignty: A case study in Indigenous data sovereignty through the East Coast Exchange.
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
Submitted timing preference: Preferably in the first week from Oct 19–24th, but we are open to discussion.
List any other organizations, collaborat: Toha Network / International Environmental Guardianship
Event description: Data sovereignty is an emerging norm for nature data, guided by frameworks like the CARE principles. As an ethical concept, it is associated with self-determination and social licence among data-sharing communities. As a practice, however, there is uncertainty about how to implement data sovereignty in the real world, especially when balancing other goods like openness, transparency, access and affordability. The East Coast Exchange (ECX) is a community-led venture that uplifts Indigenous data sovereignty by providing consent-based access to nature data for corporate reporting and disclosure. Using digital public infrastructure provided by the Toha Network, the ECX is facilitating test transactions of nature data at Te Kautuku, a Māori-owned landblock in the East Coast region of Aotearoa New Zealand. In this interactive event, representatives for Te Kautuku, ECX and Toha Network will explain the mechanisms that uplift data sovereignty, how FPIC and benefit-sharing are implemented, how community data is governed, and showcase the first bundle of nature-positive data products designed for TNFD-aligned corporate reporting and disclosure. Finally, we explore the adaptability of this data protocol for other communities and territories through global initiatives like the 8 Billion Hour Pledge.

Event title: Remote Sensing for Biodiversity Assessment and Management: From Data to Decision-Making — Armenia’s Integration into Global Observation Systems

Event description: What does it take for a country to turn Earth observation and remote sensing data into evidence decision-makers can act on? As countries work to report progress against the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) targets, a persistent gap remains between the data now available and its translation into actionable insights. Drawing on the experience of COP17 host country Armenia in developing its national ecosystems map, this session will give participants a shared, practical understanding of the full chain, from raw observation to policy-relevant evidence, building bridges between technical expertise and decision-making needs. The conversation will bring together technical and policy perspectives to examine what makes Earth observation data trustworthy, how data products can be converted into indicators that are comparable across countries, and how national governments use these indicators to update NBSAPs, track GBF targets, and direct resources where they are most needed.

Event title: Opportunities for improving ecosystem indicators for monitoring and action for 2030
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
List any other organizations, collaborat: CBD, FAO, UNSD, IUCN, The University of Melbourne
Event description: How can countries turn national data into ecosystem indicators they can actually report against? This event will identify paths towards improving the compilation of the headline indicators related to ecosystems in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), so that by the 8th national reports, all Parties are in a position to use and report on these indicators. Consistent ecosystem indicators can provide a well-rounded picture of efforts to sustain ecosystems and the services they provide (headline indicator B.1), such as how threatened they are (A.1), how much remains (A.2), is protected (3.1) and is being restored (2.1), at national scales and for groups of ecosystems globally (e.g. coral reefs or tropical rainforests). These indicators have many common foundational data needs, providing opportunities for synergistic investment in data that will be valuable across sectors. This event will explore practical solutions, partners and funding mechanisms to help fill data and knowledge gaps for ecosystems, to support GBF reporting and implementation. Through panel discussions, short presentations and Q&A, the event will introduce the indicators, take stock of challenges faced in the 7th national reports, and set out concrete proposals for overcoming those challenges. It will close by looking at the partners and funding mechanisms that can help countries develop these indicators ahead of the 8th national reports.

Event title: Enriching biodiversity data to accelerate delivery of policy- and indicator-ready data for the GBF
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
Event description:
Realizing the ambitions of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) requires more and richer data than is currently available. To track and monitor biodiversity changes over time, the GBF relies on indicators that measure progress of national biodiversity actions. To deliver the necessary evidence GBIF—the Global Biodiversity Information Facility—isenhancing its infrastructures to support richer, more complex types of biodiversity data, many
from sources newly enabled through emerging and innovative technologies. GBIF is a key infrastructure working across a range of communities including DNA-derived and disease vector data, soil and freshwater data, marine, invasive alien species and agrobiodiversity. The coming improvements will support the CBD in generating, capturing, managing and applying of primary biodiversity data needed under the GBF.
In order to do this GBIF is creating and implementing innovative new event-based data models that extend the existing infrastructure. These changes will enable more effective incorporation of data from complex monitoring initiatives that implement diverse methods including sequencing of environmental DNA, and acoustic and camera trap surveys and address known taxonomic, geographic, and temporal gaps in data coverage. The improvements will also empower the
CBD and wider policymaking community to escalate time-sensitive efforts, delivering enhanced evidence of biodiversity at the scale and speed required to implement the indicators that will measure progress towards the GBF’s objectives. This event will discuss needs and benefits of integrating richer data types across different infrastructures supporting these communities to help inform the development potential of data models to support capacity, pace and scale of biodiversity data evidence generation needed to meet incoming challenges.
This session aims to:
● Demonstrate how innovations in the GBIF infrastructure could align with other relevant data infrastructures and networks to increase data flows to fill knowledge gaps (e.g., is there a specific example we’d like to highlight?)
● Identify and explore technical tools and training needs Tools and case studies to support richer more complex types of biodiversity data
● Expand the existing biodiversity research ecosystem to a welcome broader set of biodiversity data holders
● Highlight how the new data-model makes it easier to access, use, and store more diverse types of data to provide a more complete knowledge of different forms of  biodiversity data

Event title: Connecting knowledge and data to strengthen national implementation, monitoring and reporting of the Global Biodiversity Framework
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People

Event description:
The draft Global Report on Collective Progress offers the first evidence-based assessment of implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. It highlights progress underway, while identifying persistent challenges in fragmented monitoring systems, inconsistent use of indicators, limited technical and institutional capacity, and significant data gaps.
This side event explores how countries are addressing these challenges in practice, through the National Monitoring Support Initiative, a country and region-led effort to strengthen national capacities and data systems for monitoring, reporting and decision-making on national biodiversity actions. In addition, it will showcase two complementary tools: the Knowledge Support Service for Biodiversity, connecting countries to knowledge, guidance and resources on monitoring, and the Target Tracker, helping countries access and use indicator data for reporting. In this session, participating countries, and regional partners, including Technical and Scientific Cooperation Centres (TSCCs), will demonstrate how combining tools with direct technical support, and peer-to-peer exchanges among countries facing similar challenges can help solve challenges related to national monitoring of implementation of the KMGBF. It will be relevant to countries and TSCCs in address national monitoring needs, and global indicator data providers seeking to connect their work to national monitoring efforts.

This session bridges the gap between data and decisions by showcasing how nations like Colombia, the European Union, Mozambique, and South Africa are leveraging spatial data to deliver on multiple national targets for biodiversity, climate, and land degradation. We will explore how these practical applications connect to COP17 negotiations, the draft Global Report on Collective Progress in Implementation of the KMGBF, and the IPBES Assessment on Spatial Planning and Ecological Connectivity. Event title: Armenia’s Pathway to a National Biodiversity Monitoring Framework

Event description:
Armenia is developing its national biodiversity monitoring system to support implementation of the Kunming-Montreal GBF and the country’s updated National Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan. Despite recent developments, biodiversity information remains fragmented across institutions and projects, collected using different methods and standards, and not always readily available or integrated into decision-making processes. Key challenges include strengthening long-term, coordinated monitoring; harmonizing datasets; improving data quality and interoperability; building technical capacity and ensuring that monitoring results inform conservation management and national reporting.
Our session will explore how Armenia can establish consistent long-term monitoring, connect field surveys, data digitalization, protected-area monitoring and citizen science, contribute to national reporting under the CBD, and translate data into evidence for better conservation management. The event will contribute to KMGBF Targets 20 and 21.

Event title: Ocean Biodiversity to Action: Connecting Data, Monitoring, and Decisions
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
List any other organizations, collaborat: GBIF, OBIS, GEO BON
Event description:
Marine biodiversity is being observed at unprecedented scales through environmental DNA (eDNA), autonomous platforms, satellite observations, ecological networks, fisheries surveys, natural history collections, and community-based monitoring. Despite these advances, marine biodiversity observations remain fragmented across agencies, research institutions, private organizations, and civil society, often lacking common standards and interoperable workflows. This fragmentation limits the ability to transform observations into actionable information that can effectively support conservation, management, and policy decisions. 
This event will explore how marine biodiversity data can be transformed into trusted, interoperable, decision-ready information to support implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. It will highlight the role of global and regional data infrastructures, observing networks, and monitoring programs, including OBIS, GBIF, and GOOS, in connecting observations across scales. Priorities include integrating diverse marine data streams; strengthening standards, taxonomic and genomic reference libraries, indicators, analytical tools, AI-enabled workflows; and translating biodiversity information into products that meet the needs of Parties, managers, and coastal communities. 
Emerging capabilities—including eDNA and genomics, digitized museum collections, autonomous technologies, Earth observations, and artificial intelligence—offer new opportunities to better connect observations, data infrastructures, and knowledge systems, strengthening marine biodiversity monitoring for conservation, sustainable use, restoration, and ocean management.
Outcomes of the session could include: 
Identify priority marine biodiversity data-to-decision pathways. Agree on 2–3 high-value use cases where better integration of observations, OBIS/GBIF-type infrastructures, and decision-support tools could directly improve implementation of the Global Biodiversity Framework—for example, protected-area planning, restoration, fisheries management, or tracking ecosystem change.  
Define practical interoperability needs. Produce a short list of priority gaps in standards, reference libraries, metadata, indicators, or data exchange that currently prevent marine biodiversity observations from being readily combined and used in assessments and management.  
Launch a follow-on collaboration. Identify a small group of willing organizations to develop a post-COP17 pilot or roadmap that links observing networks, data infrastructures, collections/genomics, and end users around one or more demonstration cases.

Event title: Global Concept, Local Proof: Who Decides What Counts as an OECM?
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Country/region of lead organization: Global: Offices in Kenya, Peru, Madagascar, Thailand, HQ in Switzerland
List any other organizations, collaborat: Government of Kenya – Ministry of Environment, Climate Change and Forestry (TBC); Government of Madagascar – Ministère de l’Environnement et du Développement (TBC); Durable; Government of Thailand (TBC); FAO OECMs Team; International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) (TBC); Kenya Wildlife Conservancies Association (KWCA) (TBC); International Livestock Research Institute (ILRI)
Event description:
In OECM recognition, whose evidence counts — and who decides? Under 5% of sites in the global OECM database provide supporting evidence of any kind, and only 17 of 196 CBD Parties have reported any OECM at all. Between site assessment, national recognition and international reporting lies a question that countries are answering in different ways.
This session draws on a synthesis of OECM implementation in Kenya, Madagascar and Thailand, undertaken by the Wyss Academy for Nature at the University of Bern, extended by panelists' and participants' practical experiences. It brings together national governments, conservation, community and Indigenous organizations, and researchers to examine different paths towards recognition. For example, Thailand has endorsed five business-proposed sites by government committee resolution and is building the framework for international reporting. Kenya's 160-plus community conservancies show clear potential for OECM status, but recognition as OECMs hinges on a national policy framework. Madagascar's interministerial order sets the pathway for coastal and marine sites, with terrestrial recognition still to come. Speakers and participants will explore what counts as evidence — community monitoring, citizen science, academic research, official data — and what turns a community from a site assessed into a decision-maker.
Takeaway: turning a global indicator into credible national recognition means deciding together, co-producing evidence, and co-creating real, tangible benefits to the communities who steward these landscapes.

Event title: Building the Global Ecosystems Atlas: Technology, Standards and Partnership in Action
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action

Event description:
How do diverse national datasets, satellite observations and advances in AI become trusted, decision-ready ecosystem intelligence? This session takes participants inside the technical architecture of the Global Ecosystems Atlas and the partnerships making it possible. 
The Atlas Technical Consortium brings together Ai2, ESA, Esri, Google and IUCN with the GEO Secretariat and James Cook University, combining complementary capabilities across the full ecosystem-mapping workflow - from standards, training data and foundation models to harmonisation, cloud infrastructure, validation and open access. 
Through a fast-paced technical deep dive, partners will demonstrate how these contributions connect: Ai2’s OlmoEarth Studio and OlmoEarth foundation models; ESA’s WEED toolbox, national mapping and cross-referencing work; Esri’s geoprocessing and data-distribution infrastructure; and IUCN’s Global Ecosystem Typology and scientific standards. 
The session will show how this integrated workflow turns fragmented ecosystem data into an open, interoperable global resource, while inviting technical teams, mapping agencies and data partners to help shape the Global Ecosystems Atlas as it moves from ecosystem extent mapping towards monitoring change and condition.

Event title: Introducing the Atlas of Ungulate Migration: a data-driven tool to conserve terrestrial migrations
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: UN Convention on Migratory Species
Event description:
In the face of rapid anthropogenic development, many of the world’s remaining terrestrial migrations are being truncated or lost before we have adequate maps to describe the animals’ habitats, seasonal ranges, and routes. In response to this growing threat, the Global Initiative on Ungulate Migration built the first digital Atlas of Ungulate Migration: a repository for publicly available migration maps incorporating the best available science on migratory populations around the world. Implemented under the auspices of the UN Convention on Migratory Species (CMS), the Atlas now hosts 50+ migration maps and accompanying fact sheets from species as diverse as khulan in the Mongolian Gobi, guanaco in the Argentine Patagonia and the white-eared kob in South Sudan.
In this event, we will introduce the Atlas of Ungulate Migration as a data-driven resource for countries, decision-makers, and spatial planners aiming to maintain connectivity for migratory land mammals. Based on our extensive mapping of migration corridors, we will also present new research revealing key patterns and insights with implications for large-scale land management, conservation and connectivity initiatives. Significant opportunities exist for countries to improve the conservation of migratory wildlife through stronger management of key habitats and movement-related conflicts based on newly available derived data products.

Event title: Using Biodiversity Data and the Mitigation Hierarchy to Inform Conservation and Development Decisions
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: GEO BON
Event description:
Biodiversity data provide a strong foundation for informed decision-making and the sustainable management of natural resources. This session will showcase examples from infrastructure development projects in Brazil and Peru where the Mitigation Hierarchy was applied to collect, analyze, and use biodiversity data to avoid, minimize, and restore impacts on biodiversity. These science-based approaches contributed to highly successful conservation outcomes and ultimately informed the development of national policies, demonstrating how evidence-based decision-making can influence conservation and development at broader scales.
Through a series of case studies, the speakers will highlight how practical and cost-effective approaches to reducing habitat fragmentation have inspired private sector managers, Indigenous communities, academics, and other local stakeholders. In Peru, documentation of wildlife use of natural canopy bridges in forested landscapes led to the design and implementation of artificial canopy bridges in Brazil, which have since been incorporated into national guidelines for future development projects.
The session will also present innovative monitoring approaches that, for the first time, documented how measures to avoid, minimize, and restore biodiversity impacts during development projects can directly inform management decisions. These efforts helped build local conservation capacity, strengthen technical knowledge, and support adaptive management practices. The resulting methodologies were subsequently adopted as national policy, illustrating how biodiversity monitoring can drive lasting improvements in both conservation and sustainable development. These approaches and methodologies also offer a potential framework for tracking, quantifying, and accelerating progress toward the targets of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Event description:
Countries are mandated to track their progress toward the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework using indicators that summarize biodiversity trends. Many still face fragmented monitoring efforts, technical barriers, limited access to data and tools, and gaps in capacity. BON in a Box, an open-source GEO BON platform that helps countries build the capacity to calculate their own indicators and strengthen their national reporting.
This session shows how BON in a Box delivers scientifically rigorous and transparent solutions to these reporting challenges. We will present recent progress that has strengthened the robustness of our mission: a choice between an online user space or a local install for complete ownership of your own data, updated biodiversity indicator workflows, AI-assisted features that support users through their analyses, ongoing collaborations with Parties, scientists, and other organizations.
Through short presentations and demonstrations, followed by an open discussion, the session will show how we are building lasting national capacity through reproducible workflows that connect data to decisions. We will also highlight where collaboration and investment will expand this work.

Event title: Diversifying Knowledge, Diversifying Life: Genetic Diversity for Resilience and Equitable Connection of Knowledge Systems for Change
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: University of Zurich, SNSF, WWF Schweiz, Stiftung Lanschaftsschutz, Wilnispark Zürich, KORA, CIMMYT Mexico, Naitonal Bioresource Project Wheat, Japan
Event description:
This session consists of two parts:
Part I. 16:30-17:00 (talk) Genetic diversity in crops for resilience (Kentaro Shimizu)
Genetic diversity within a crop species is essential for protecting biodiversity and ensuring food security. This talk highlights research projects that filled a knowledge gap in shaping sustainable agriculture. We showed that underexplored wheat landraces (traditional varieties) from Asia preserved by the National BioResource Project (NBRP), Japan, are valuable sources of disease resistance and drought tolerance. These findings highlight the importance of seed stock centers (ex situ conservation) and of preserving landraces by local farmers (in situ conservation). Furthermore, a cultivar mixture could reduce herbivore damage, which can lead to reduced use of pesticides.
Part II. 17:00-18:30 (workshop) Methodologies for equitably connecting knowledge systems to address socio-ecological problems (Sierra Deutsch)
While KMGBF Target 21 mandates inclusion of traditional and local knowledge, gaps remain in equitably connecting knowledge systems. This interactive workshop introduces methods for weaving Indigenous, practitioner, and academic knowledge in parity, avoiding knowledge subordination and extractive data practices. Using adapted versions of the Three Horizons Framework and Two-Eyed Seeing, participants will work with their own field projects to co-develop assessment methods for transformative approaches to socio-ecological problems. Attendees will also learn Protocols, Practices, and Methods (PPMs) that equalize science-society collaborations and reduce epistemic bias in conservation design, leaving with a replicable toolkit to operationalize Targets 20, 21, and 22.

Event title: From Biodiversity Data to Connected Landscapes: Taiwan’s Ecological Network for Biodiversity Conservation and Climate Resilience
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Submitted timing preference: Any time apart from Wednesday, 28 October 13:00–14:00
Event description: Global environmental change has placed ecosystem integrity at the forefront of international conservation priorities, as intact ecosystems underpin long-term ecological resilience. While the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) explicitly calls for ecologically representative and well-connected conservation networks, implementation remains challenging in densely populated lowland landscapes, where intense land-use competition constrains opportunities for protected area expansion. Since 2018, Taiwan has responded by extending its conservation focus beyond high-elevation ecosystems towards a spatially integrated lowland conservation network. This transition is operationalized through the Taiwan Ecological Network (TEN), a science-based, multi-scale framework that translates biodiversity data into spatial conservation priorities. Species occurrence data mobilized through TaiBIF, Taiwan's GBIF node, together with the cross-sectoral biodiversity databases, were used to model species distributions and identify biodiversity hotspots and threatened-species habitats. These data-informed spatial layers contributed to the delineation of 44 priority biodiversity areas at the landscape scale and 45 conservation corridors strengthening ecological connectivity at the regional scale, complemented by place-based governance supporting nature-positive action at the site scale. TEN further advances a whole-of-government and whole-of-society approach through OECMs, an ESG project-matching platform, and partnerships with Indigenous Peoples and Local Communities (IPLCs). Collectively, TEN demonstrates how national biodiversity data infrastructure can support the operationalization of GBF Target 3 through coordinated, multi-scale spatial planning and connectivity-focused governance, strengthening ecological resilience under ongoing environmental change.

Event title: Defenders at Risk: Closing the Gap on Target 22 and Environmental Human Rights Data
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: IWGIA, AIPP, OHCHR, ICCA Consortium, Global Witness, Natural Justice, FPP, ALLIED
Event description: Target 22 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework explicitly calls for the protection of environmental human rights defenders (EHRDs), recognizing them as central to biodiversity conservation. Yet the first global review of KM-GBF progress found EHRD protection to be the weakest-reported element of Target 22: only 13% of Parties addressed it in their national targets. This gap sits alongside a well-documented pattern of violence — OHCHR estimates nearly 6,000 defenders killed or disappeared since 2015, with environmental defenders and Indigenous communities disproportionately affected, and civil society networks recording hundreds of killings and thousands of non-lethal attacks in the last two years alone. This session brings together UN agencies, data collectors, Indigenous Peoples, local communities, women defenders and Party representatives to examine what the reporting gap reveals about national priorities, share evidence on the scale and patterns of attacks in biodiversity-rich regions, explore the links between defender protection, participation and land rights, and identify concrete steps Parties can take before COP18 — improving reporting, strengthening legal frameworks, and mainstreaming EHRD protection in NBSAPs.

Event title: Where Learning Happens: Science of Where + Science of Conservation + Power of Education
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Submitted timing preference: Thu 22 Oct from 10-11am (time is blocked off in the "Data Pavilion Spreadsheet"
List any other organizations, collaborat: IUCN Commission for Communication and Education, National Geographic, Children of Armenia Fund
Event description:
Geographic Information Systems (GIS) is a powerful enabler of nature-based education by connecting environmental learning with real-world data, spatial thinking, and community action. International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) seeks to expand access to Nature-based Education, including access to maps, data, and learning resources that help students, educators, and conservation practitioners better understand ecosystems and identify where conservation action is needed. 
At the classroom level, National Geographic MapMaker provides an accessible entry point to spatial learning, enabling educators and students to explore environmental and cultural topics through interactive maps and curated geographic content. Beyond formal education systems, innovative programs such as the Children of Armenia Fund’s “Map the Future” initiative demonstrate how GIS can empower rural youth to address local challenges related to agriculture, disaster preparedness, and resource planning through hands-on mapping and analysis.  
Together, these efforts illustrate how GIS supports biodiversity action through capacity-building and development (Target 20), training and knowledge exchange, and the strengthening of networks and institutional capacity. Join us to learn how equipping students and educators’ geospatial nature-based education can build the next generation of biodiversity stewards and informed decision-makers.

Event title: Connecting Law and Biodiversity Data for Action
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
Event description:
Biodiversity data helps us understand what is changing in nature. Legal data helps us understand who has authority to respond, what protections apply, and which actions the law requires or permits. Connecting these evidence types can help turn observations into better-informed decisions.
This session will introduce Legal Atlas and its approach to organizing, mapping, and comparing legal information. Together with GEO BON, we will explore opportunities to connect legal information with biodiversity data and analysis through BON in a Box. Examples will illustrate questions such a connection could help answer: Where do ecological pressures coincide with gaps in legal protection? Which institutions have responsibility to act? Where could further legal analysis support conservation priorities?
The discussion will also address a funding challenge: building and maintaining connections across legal research, biodiversity monitoring, and public decision-making can fall between conventional funding categories.
Designed for policymakers, researchers, practitioners, and funders, the session aims to identify useful starting points for collaboration and explore support for shared tools and sustained data maintenance. Its central message is that connecting evidence about nature with evidence about law can strengthen the path from data to action.

Event title: From data to reporting to action: implementing the genetic diversity indicators of the KMGBF
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: UK, France, Bosnia and Herzegovina, IUCN, GEO BON, UZH, Coalition for Conservation Genetics, South Africa
Event description:
Genetic diversity is essential for the persistence and adaptive capacity of species and populations. It is explicitly included in Goal A and Target 4 of the KMGBF, and with several indicators. As Parties move forward with their monitoring and reporting, a key question is how available biodiversity information can be translated into practical genetic diversity indicators and then into conservation decisions.
This interactive session will bring together Parties and the conservation genetics community to share practical experience with implementing the KMGBF genetic diversity indicators. 
First, a short introduction will provide accessible orientation to the indicators and the diverse data that can support them (population monitoring, GBIF and national datasets, landcover and satellite data, ecological information, and genetic data). 
Second, representatives working with Parties will share how they approached genetic diversity monitoring and reporting in practice: who was involved, how decisions were made, what information and data was available, and what they learned through the process.
Third, the session will highlight practical, freely available resources available to support monitoring, indicator assessment, and implementation, while avoiding a one-size-fits-all approach. 
Last, moderated discussion and audience input will identify questions, data and knowledge gaps, and priorities for future guidance and capacity development. 
In summary, Parties can begin genetic diversity monitoring with data, information and expertise that already exist, while an international community (including from UZH and GEO BON and partners) is available to help Parties move from data to reporting indicator values and action.

Event title: Taking Action for Nature, Together: The Next Decade of Conservation Management
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Submitted timing preference: 1st: Thu 22 Oct 13:15–14:45. 2nd: Wed 21 Oct 13:15–14:45. 30 min acceptable.
List any other organizations, collaborat: WWF Armenia (host-country partner); Zoological Society of London (ZSL); Re:wild; Allen Institute for AI (Ai2); with participation from SMART-EarthRanger Conservation Alliance member organizations and practitioner institutions from Armenia, Africa, Asia, and Latin America.
Type of event: Moderated panel with practitioner-led field demonstration
Event description:
Every commitment in the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework rests on a question the global review will now ask: can we show what is happening on the ground, consistently, at scale? Sites record data differently, baselines rarely align, and evidence rarely reaches national reporting.
The SMART-EarthRanger Conservation Alliance, active today across more than 2,000 sites in over 100 countries, is building a different future: one shared foundation for conservation management. One shared data model, so a patrol report from the Caucasus and a collar reading from the Congo Basin can be combined and compared. Standardized baselines, so progress toward 30x30 can be measured consistently. An open foundation that new and emerging technologies can build on. And the training, support, and shared services that turn adoption into outcomes.
Co-hosted with WWF Armenia, this session brings rangers, protected area authorities, and government agencies from the Caucasus, Africa, Asia, and Latin America to describe what that future means on the ground: safer field personnel, human-wildlife conflict addressed before it escalates, and site-level evidence that strengthens national reporting while staying owned by those who collect it. Participants will leave knowing how their sites and agencies can start with SERCA today and collect standardized, comparable data.

Lead organization: Rede Nacional de Ensino e Pesquisa - RNP (SiBBr)
Event title: A proposal for differentiated access to socio-biodiversity data
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: Ministry of Science, Technology and Innovation - MCTI
Event description: Restricted Access Species Data (RASD) requires a clear distinction regarding the reasons for limiting access. We highlight three aspects that lead communities to restrict access: 1. preventing information on species properties and uses from fueling commercial products without free, prior, and informed consent. In this case, the proposal is to make only basic metadata publicly available, while detailed information on species and their uses remains restricted; external access would require a formal request, community approval, and an agreement on terms of use and liability; 2. knowledge related to religious or sacred practices may require total restriction, in which case data systematization would serve the sole purpose of preserving that knowledge; 3. information regarding species used for subsistence hunting can be sensitive, even when such practices are permitted under existing legal and community frameworks. However, precise taxonomic, temporal, and spatial data may be essential for population monitoring and sustainable management. Thus, access could be authorized for third parties to support management efforts. The proposed model combines FAIR and CARE principles through access classifications, community authority, purpose-based permissions, and traceability. The goal is to facilitate conservation and public policy without depriving communities of control over their knowledge, territories, and practices.

Event title: Agents for nature: what happens when the field's expertise can answer back
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: World Resources Institute (Global Nature Watch), United States; Conservation X Labs, United States
Event description:
Around the world, hundreds of organizations track forests, fisheries, mangroves, wildlife, pollution, and ice. Each holds deep expertise the rest of the field needs. Yet putting that expertise to work takes resources most organizations don’t have: analyst time, technical staff, and the hours it takes to turn raw data into an answer someone can act on.
AI agents are starting to change that. Skylight’s Shippy gives maritime analysts sourced intelligence in minutes, and EarthRanger’s Atlas does the same for protected areas. Each gives a small team another staff member: one that extends data fluency across the organization and surfaces insights previously out of reach. But conservation moves at the speed of trust. This session will explore lessons learned: what worked, what broke, and the ethical guardrails that keep agents honest, in check, and humans at the center of every decision. It will consider what organizations without engineering teams need, where agents still fall short in the field, and what practitioners trust an agent with and what they keep in human hands. The session will also look toward where the field is heading: agents that interoperate across organizations, so the best available expertise on any question is one conversation away, attributed to its source, and earned through trust.

Event title: From designation to delivery — resourcing the data layer of the regional and subregional technical and scientific cooperation support centres
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Event description:
In CBD Decision 15/8, the Parties set up regional and subregional technical and scientific cooperation support centres. A key role of these centres is to catalyse and support technical and scientific cooperation projects and programmes that help people access and use available scientific knowledge, information and data.
This side event builds on the session held at COP16 and reports on progress since then. It will look at how data access and use differ across regions under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF). It will also show how the regional networks of GBIF, the Global Biodiversity Information Facility, can be organised into service models that centres can hold, fund and deliver. These service models respond to new reporting requirements that call for better systems for gathering and repackaging biodiversity data.
Since COP16, GBIF has worked with four centres one by one, starting from what each committed to in its published workplan: SPREP, SANBI, CARICOM and IUCN's Asia centre. This session brings that work back to all the centres together.
The presentations and discussions will focus on:
-The centres' data and information needs, and where those needs are not yet met
-Practical technical and capacity solutions for accessing and exchanging relevant data, such as species baselines, standards and shared infrastructure, data mobilization and in-region technical support, and what each one makes possible for centres and the Parties they serve
-A framework for collaboration between the GBIF network and the support centres, and sustainable scaling-up of national biodiversity facilities so centres can deliver on capacity-building and on technical and scientific cooperation
Expected outcomes:
-A shared picture of regional data needs, prioritised by the centres
The centres' confirmation of which service areas matter most, tested against worked examples from the Pacific and southern Africa
-A common set of core functions and service areas for centres to build on
-Ways for centres to fund this work, and the partnerships needed to deliver it

Event title: From Biodiversity Data to One Health Action: Connecting Knowledge Systems for Pandemic Prevention and Resilient Landscapes
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: IUCN CEM, PREZODE, TNC, WOAH, Future Earth
Event description:
The implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and the CBD Global Action Plan on Biodiversity and Health provides an important opportunity to better connect biodiversity monitoring with One Health decision-making. Biodiversity loss, deforestation, habitat fragmentation, land-use change, wildlife exploitation and climate change can affect human, animal, plant and ecosystem health and contribute to emerging disease risks. Yet biodiversity observations, environmental and land-use data, animal and human health surveillance, and knowledge held by Indigenous Peoples and local communities are often collected or held through separate institutions and systems. This fragmentation limits our ability to identify priorities and translate knowledge into timely preventive action.
This event will explore how these complementary data and knowledge systems can be better connected to generate actionable evidence for One Health action. Through practical examples and an interactive discussion, speakers will demonstrate how biodiversity, ecological, spatial and wildlife health monitoring, together with community-led surveillance, can support risk assessment, early warning and decisions for biodiversity conservation, ecosystem management and zoonotic disease prevention at source. 
Key messages are that monitoring should respond to clearly identified decision needs; evidence must be interpreted in its ecological and social context; and effective action requires collaboration, equitable data governance and community participation. The discussion will identify practical lessons for Parties implementing biodiversity and health priorities.

Lead organization: Sustainability & Climate Change Programme (SCCP), Université des Mascareignes
Event title: The First Mauritius Atlas of Terrestrial Ecosystems: ecosystem extent and condition mapping for decision makers
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: Dr. Prakash (Sanju) Deenapanray (SCCP)
Event description: The island of Mauritius was once entirely covered by forests. Today, nearly 60% of the island’s land surface has been converted to agriculture, urban areas, and infrastructure, a transformation driven by over three centuries of land use changes. Up to now, the condition of the island’s remaining ecosystems had never been comprehensively mapped or measured. Using the UN System of Environmental-Economic Accounting – Ecosystem Accounting (SEEA-EA) framework and open-access earth observation data, it presents the first spatialised extent and condition accounts for terrestrial ecosystems of Mauritius. Tracing the island’s geological origins, climatic gradients, and watershed networks, it reconstructs the natural landscape as a reference point, documents the dynamics of land cover change, and measures the current condition of the island’s ecosystems relative to their pristine state. Aggregated to administrative boundaries at national, district, and village council levels, the Atlas translates ecological data into a practical decision support tool; providing government, landowners, planners, and civil society with a shared baseline for prioritising restoration, directing investment, and informing land use planning in support of biodiversity, sustainable land management, and climate commitments

Event title: Transition risk: what your biodiversity data reveals
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
Submitted timing preference: Oct 21, 22, 23: any time of day is fine; Oct 24: 11 AM - 4:30 PM
List any other organizations, collaborat: IBAT
Event description:
Many types of biodiversity datasets exist, but which ones actually connect to business risk, and to the decisions finance and sustainability teams need to make? Planning for nature transition risk means connecting the dots between data and risk.
In this joint presentation with Dunya Analytics and IBAT, we will walk through the categories of data that make up a comprehensive biodiversity risk assessment. These are aligned with TNFD criteria for sensitive locations, and include protected and conserved areas, key biodiversity areas, and areas of high or rapidly declining ecosystem integrity. Each data category will be connected to specific transition risks, from regulatory exposure to shifting market expectations, and grounded in real business decisions and financial outcomes companies are already facing.
Attendees will leave with a clear framework for identifying which biodiversity datasets matter for their own risk assessments, and how to translate that data into decisions their finance and sustainability teams can act on.
To ground this in practice, we will conduct a risk assessment using the Dunya Analytics platform with integrated IBAT data for a specific location and show in real time how the data categories discussed translate into flagged risks.

Event title: Living data for action and equity
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
Submitted timing preference: Fri Oct 23, Sat Oct 24, Mon Oct 26
List any other organizations, collaborat: GEO, GEO BON, GBIF, Smithsonian, and all Pavilion members
Event description: Data is never neutral — who collects it, who can access it, and how it is used all shape whose interests get protected. This event brings together five stations to examine biodiversity data through that lens: from the social and cultural values embedded in how we define "nature," to new technologies expanding who can monitor biodiversity, to concrete threats — natural hazards and invasive species — that demand better data to act on. Across formats ranging from open conversation to interactive demos to art installation, the event asks not just what the data shows, but who it serves and how it can drive equitable, forward-looking action. This is an interactive session where participants interact with five stations (1) ask a scientist / tell a scientist: we will engage on exchange between participatns and scientists on examples, needs, dat sovereignty and other toics regarding living data for action and equity, (2) Why We Need Critical Social Sciences for Effective Decision-Making: What is the definition of nature and why does it matter? At this interactive station, participants will explore the many different (individual and cultural) definitions of nature and how this influences how we relate to it. Taking this a step further, the station will stimulate reflection on how and why certain definitions and relations get prioritized, for whom, and why these questions matter for a sustainable and biodiverse future..; (3) Can New Monitoring Technologies Make Biodiversity Data More Accessible? Low-cost, automated tools such as acoustic sensors can expand biodiversity monitoring across space and time while reducing some of the financial and logistical barriers to data collection. In this interactive demonstration, participants trigger an animal sound, see it captured by an AudioMoth and translated into a biodiversity observation, and follow the pathway from sound to data, evidence and action. The station also highlights that technology alone is not enough: equitable use of biodiversity data still depends on shared standards, infrastructure, analytical capacity and political alignment. (4) what about risk: A Global Map of Species at Risk of Extinction Due to Natural Hazards. This station presents new evidence showing which species and areas may be particularly vulnerable to hazards such as hurricanes and other extreme events, and how these risks may evolve under future climate change. By bringing this overlooked dimension of extinction risk into the discussion, the study provides a first approximation of where conservation attention may be most urgently needed. The findings can help policymakers and conservation practitioners better anticipate emerging threats, identify priorities, and target efforts to safeguard vulnerable species.  5. get a break and explore INVASIVA:The INVASIVA artwork expands along a projected trajectory from IPBES, GRIIS, and IvaCost data, making us feel the facts about the future global economic and ecological impacts of invasive alien species. WOVEN uses the power of art and culture as a catalyst for the science that makes our planet thrive. We make complex environmental issues accessible, understandable and personal — reaching the heads of state and the hearts of the public

Event title: Toward a World Biodiversity Research Programme: strengthening global scientific coordination to support implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: GEO BON, CBD secretariat, University of Potsdam, University of Connecticut, CREAF, UKCEH, Kingdom of the Netherlands, UNEP-WCMC
Event description:
Climate science has the World Climate Research Programme. What is the equivalent for biodiversity?
The draft Global Report on Collective Progress highlights persistent gaps in knowledge, monitoring, modelling, data access, and scientific capacity that constrain implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KM-GBF). While biodiversity science has advanced rapidly and IPBES has strengthened the science-policy interface, research remains fragmented across regions, disciplines, and institutions. Many policy-relevant knowledge gaps identified by Parties and assessments are not translated into coordinated international research priorities, and many countries still face barriers to generating and using the evidence needed for implementation and reporting.
This workshop will explore whether a World Biodiversity Research Programme (WBRP) could help address this gap. Inspired by the World Climate Research Programme, and complementing existing institutions, a WBRP would coordinate biodiversity research in support of policy needs by translating knowledge gaps into shared research priorities, supporting common monitoring and modelling frameworks, strengthening capacity and collaboration, and promoting leadership from the Global South and Indigenous Peoples and local communities.
Participants will discuss the rationale for a WBRP, consider options for a three-year pilot consultation process, and explore priorities, opportunities, risks, and governance arrangements. The discussion will test whether stronger global coordination of biodiversity research could accelerate KM-GBF implementation and deliver more effective, equitable, and policy-relevant science.

Event title: Turning Data into Decisions: The Role of GIS in Biodiversity Action
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: Map of Life Solutions, SFI, Mobi/Insights
Event description:
Transforming biodiversity data into actionable decisions is essential for achieving the goals of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF). GIS plays a powerful role in bringing together disparate biodiversity data, from field observations and siloed national datasets to global information resources, and transforming them into integrated, easy-to-use decision support systems that inform conservation policy, planning, and management.
This session explores how GIS is helping organizations turn biodiversity information into meaningful action at national, regional, and global scales. Yale's Map of Life Solutions is working with countries such as Guyana to develop holistic biodiversity information platforms that strengthen national policy, guide conservation priorities, and support progress toward global biodiversity goals. These same capabilities are helping organizations make more informed land-management decisions, including the Sustainable Forestry Initiative (SFI), which is advancing the use of biodiversity information to support sustainable forest management and healthier, more resilient ecosystems. Building on these examples, Esri's Global Biodiversity and Conservation Hexagons demonstrate how diverse biodiversity, conservation, and environmental datasets can be integrated into standardized, analysis-ready geographic units, providing a consistent foundation for understanding conditions, identifying priorities, and tracking progress toward global biodiversity targets.

Event title: It takes a village…or a state, or province or territory to achieve 30x30
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: IUCN North America, California, Quebec, Catalonia
Event description:
Achieving the global 30x30 target will depend not only on national commitments, but on the leadership, innovation, and sustained action of subnational governments. States, provinces, and territories are uniquely positioned to translate ambitious biodiversity goals into measurable outcomes through land and marine conservation, data-driven decision making, partnerships with Indigenous Peoples and local communities, and long-term stewardship. As the world enters the final years before the 2030 deadline, subnational organizations are demonstrating how conservation can move beyond protected area designation toward effective management, equitable governance, and lasting ecological impact.

This session will showcase the High Ambition Coalition Subnational Government Task Force’s effort to foster a global community of practice around 30x30 to raise awareness of current status toward the goal and accelerate progress.  Fortunately, subnational governments are advancing 30x30 implementation through practical strategies, collaborative governance models, and investments in data and geospatial tools for visualization, planning and monitoring. Featuring actions in jurisdictions including California, Quebec, Catalonia, Scotland, and Pará, panelists will share lessons learned and discuss challenges and opportunities. By elevating the experiences of subnational leaders, the session will showcase scalable approaches that can accelerate progress toward biodiversity conservation goals while strengthening partnerships across all levels of government and society.

Event title: Connecting Forests and Collections: Building a Digital Infrastructure for Biodiversity
Paired thematic focus: Weekend — requested dates only
List any other organizations, collaborat: Kew Gardens, GBIF, MOBOT, Cornell, etc. (still TBC)
Event description:
We are entering an era of unprecedented biodiversity data. Living forests generate observations through long-term plots, remote sensing, acoustic monitoring, environmental DNA, and other emerging technologies. Meanwhile, herbaria, botanical gardens, museums, genomic laboratories, and global databases hold centuries of information about species identity, distribution, traits, and evolutionary history. Yet these valuable data sources remain largely disconnected.
This panel will explore how GEO-TREES could help bridge that divide, linking data collected from trees in tropical forests with digitized herbarium specimens, taxonomic records, genomic information, and other biodiversity datasets. Creating these connections could improve species identification, reveal changes in forest composition, strengthen biodiversity and carbon estimates, and enable scientists to track ecological responses to climate and land-use change at unprecedented scales. The discussion will consider the scientific standards, partnerships, governance models, and technologies needed to create an interoperable system that serves researchers and tropical countries alike. Potential collaborators could include Kew Gardens, GBIF, the New York Botanical Garden, the Missouri Botanical Garden, Cornell University, and UK-based environmental DNA laboratories.
By connecting physical specimens, molecular evidence, field observations, and digital tools, GEO-TREES could become more than a forest-monitoring network: it could provide essential global infrastructure for understanding and protecting tropical biodiversity.

Event title: Maldives National Accelerator: From Ecosystem Data to Country Action
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance

List any other organizations, collaborat: Maldives Ministry of Environment, Ai2, DEFRA
Event description:
What does it take for a country to build a trusted, nationally owned ecosystem map - and what becomes possible once it has one? This session takes a practical deep dive into the Maldives, the first National Accelerator of the Global Ecosystems Atlas, launched through a partnership between the Maldives Ministry of Environment and the Group on Earth Observations, supported by the United Kingdom through Defra. 
Representatives from the Maldives, the Global Ecosystems Atlas and partners will walk through how the country developed its national ecosystem map, harmonised with the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology, combining national expertise with Earth observation data, open methods and targeted technical support. The discussion will explore what the process required in practice, the challenges encountered, and how the resulting ecosystem intelligence can support national reporting, spatial and marine planning, conservation and restoration, and better-targeted investment. 
The session will then look beyond the Maldives at what elements of the National Accelerator can be replicated elsewhere, how national capacity can be strengthened, and what's needed to help more countries move from fragmented ecosystem information to operational, nationally owned mapping. 
With the approach now extending to Papua New Guinea, the Maldives offers a concrete demonstration of how the Global Ecosystems Atlas can translate global methods into practical country delivery.

Event title: Beyond Commitments: Real-World Biodiversity Monitoring for Business, Conservation, and Policy
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance

Event description:
As governments, companies, and investors increase their commitments to biodiversity, a critical question remains: how can we measure outcomes in ways that are credible, practical, and useful for decision-making?
This session will explore real-world approaches to biodiversity monitoring, drawing on lessons from FSC's Fast-Tracking Biodiversity Impact Assessment initiative and complementary experiences from forest companies, technology providers, and biodiversity experts. Panelists will discuss how organizations are combining field inventories, remote sensing, geospatial technologies, environmental DNA (eDNA), and other innovative tools to assess biodiversity outcomes across production and conservation landscapes. The session will also showcase how Esri StoryMaps can help communicate biodiversity monitoring results in ways that make complex information more accessible and actionable.
Beyond the technologies themselves, the discussion will focus on implementation: what has worked, what has proven difficult, and what lessons have emerged from applying biodiversity monitoring approaches in real-world settings. Speakers will share experiences balancing locally relevant data with globally consistent methodologies, meeting the needs of policymakers and market actors, and scaling monitoring efforts across diverse landscapes.
Participants will leave with a clearer understanding of emerging best practices for biodiversity monitoring and how technology, partnerships, and practical lessons from the field can help accelerate implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Event title: From Metrics to Strategy: Why Biodiversity Must Become a Business Priority
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance

Event description:
As biodiversity rises on the corporate and financial agenda, organizations increasingly need reliable information to understand their impacts, dependencies, risks and opportunities related to nature. Yet many still face challenges in transforming biodiversity data into meaningful decisions, effective management actions and credible disclosures.
Bringing together representatives from the LIFE Coalition, leading companies, financial institutions and biodiversity experts, this session will explore how robust, comparable and decision-relevant biodiversity data can support business strategy, risk management, target setting and reporting.
Through practical examples, participants will discuss how the LIFE System enables organizations to monitor biodiversity performance, generate consistent information and support decision-making across sectors. By connecting biodiversity monitoring, management and reporting through a standardized approach, the LIFE System helps bridge the gap between data collection, indicators and decision-making. The session will demonstrate how standardized biodiversity metrics provide a common language for measurement and reporting, enhancing the quality, credibility, transparency and comparability of biodiversity disclosures, while supporting companies in aligning with Target 15 and frameworks such as TNFD.
The event will conclude with the launch of the LIFE Coalition Statement, a collective call to action advocating for the integration of biodiversity into corporate and financial strategies and highlighting the critical role of data-driven decision-making in the transition to a nature-positive economy.

Event title: Biodiversity Data in Practice: Connecting Monitoring, Management and Reporting with LIFE Key
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions

Organizations are collecting increasing amounts of biodiversity information, yet many still struggle to translate this data into management priorities, strategic decisions and measurable outcomes.
This session will demonstrate how LIFE Key helps bridge this gap by connecting biodiversity monitoring, management and reporting within a single standardized environment. Through a live demonstration and practical examples from different sectors, participants will explore how organizations can collect, organize and analyze biodiversity information to better understand their impacts, dependencies, risks and opportunities related to nature.
The session will showcase how standardized metrics and a common assessment framework improve the consistency, comparability and usability of biodiversity information, helping organizations track performance, set targets and support decision-making. Participants will also learn how LIFE Key generates reliable and auditable information that can strengthen biodiversity disclosures and support alignment with Target 15 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, as well as frameworks such as TNFD.
Beyond reporting, the demonstration will highlight how company-level biodiversity information can contribute to broader biodiversity monitoring efforts and help organizations move from data collection to informed action. The key message is that effective biodiversity management depends on turning data into practical insights that enable organizations to monitor, manage and demonstrate their biodiversity performance over time.

Event title: From data to reporting to action: how Galaxy Ecology initiative allows to design a sustainable model to manage and boost indicator production from local to global
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions
List any other organizations, collaborat: French BON, Data Terra french research infrastructure, Data Terra European Open Science Cloud node, CCAMLR french scientific delegation, MNHN, CNRS, IRD, INRAE, Laurent Durieux, Sabrina Krief, Myriam Heuertz, Emma Inthavong, Jian-Sheng Sun, Germany, Gabon, République du Congo, New Zealand, United Kingdom, Belgium
Event description:
Data integration in biodiversity science is complex, essentially because  framework harmonizing data and methods is lacking. Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs) represent a relevant framework for identifying appropriate data to be collated and for creating and implementing analytical workflows, from raw data to EBV data products.
The aim of the Galaxy Ecology initiative is to operationalize EBV indicators by targeting the highest levels of FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperability, Reusable) for source code implementation, so that data and tools can be widely shared and reused. 
The French Biodiversity data hub of Data Terra research infrastructure, MNHN and IRD are proposing a workshop allowing to showcase mature open source tools and computational workflows to produce Biodiversity metrics and indicators from genes to ecosystems, in terrestrial as marine biomes.
First, we will introduce the Galaxy Ecology initiative, a web platform to get, process, analyze and visualize biodiversity data and then the French BON EBV operationalization pilot based on it.
Second, concrete and diverse Galaxy computational workflows will be showcased starting with the One Forest Vision initiative for the forest and wetlands of the 3 tropical bassins, CCAMLR for Antarctic conservation, European Biodiversa+ GINAMO project to illustrate genetic diversity indicators production, Gaia Data and One Water for national implementation and finally MOOREV and EVALABLOC for local applications using citizen sciences.
Third, we will show how Galaxy Ecology is more than a platform: it is a crossroads for open science communities, enabling the sharing of data, code, efforts and resources from local to global scales, while providing a sustainable foundation for itself and more recent, fragile initiatives such as Bon in a Box pipelines.
Finally, a discussion with audience inputs will allow to identify gaps and priorities for future development.
