Event description: The Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework requires countries to monitor changes in natural ecosystems, notably through Headline Indicator A.2 on the Extent of Natural Ecosystems. However, many Parties face technical and capacity challenges in producing consistent ecosystem maps and reporting against the GBF monitoring framework. Advances in Earth Observation, cloud computing, artificial intelligence and open data infrastructures offer new opportunities for scalable, cost-effective and repeatable ecosystem monitoring. This Pavilion event will present the World Ecosystem Extent Dynamics (WEED) project, funded by ESA, led by VITO, and implemented in collaboration with EEA, UNSD and GEO. WEED provides an open-source, cloud-based toolbox for mapping and monitoring terrestrial, freshwater and coastal ecosystems, aligned with the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology and supporting GBF Headline Indicator A.2 and SEEA Ecosystem Accounting. The solution has been co-developed with national authorities in Norway, Czechia, Greece, Colombia, South Africa and Vietnam, and is being extended to Slovakia, Georgia, the Philippines, Cameroon and Uganda. The event will combine an introduction to the policy context, a presentation of the WEED toolbox, and country experiences highlighting the benefits and challenges of integrating the WEED toolbox into national biodiversity monitoring and NBSAPs. An interactive panel with participating countries, ESA, IUCN, the WEED consortium and the GEO Global Ecosystem Atlas initiative will discuss how interoperable, open-source EO solutions can strengthen national capacities, reduce monitoring costs, improve production of Headline Indicator A.2 and support consistent GBF reporting.

Event title: Earth Observation for high-integrity nature markets
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation
List any other organizations, collaborat: University of Oxford, TNFD, DG ENV
Event description: Scaling nature finance requires moving from modelled assumptions to verified, spatial reality. This side event explores how Earth Observation (EO) can enable a range of nature finance mechanisms. The session will discuss findings from ESA’s LEON project as a practical example on how EO data and tools can provide transparent and standardized evidence, bridge data gaps and improving decision-making. EO can also foster confidence for finance actors to participate in nature finance mechanisms, and facilitate implementation by demonstrating additionality, checking compliance, and communicating outcomes more transparently. The event will discuss EO in the context of corporate disclosure frameworks like the TNFD to assess environmental risks and dependencies. It will also explore the high-integrity data and monitoring needs to support emerging market mechanisms, aligned with policy initiatives like DG ENV’s Nature Credits Roadmap. The conversation will focus on current data gaps, practical integration challenges, and discuss future steps towards the standardized use of EO data to operationalise nature finance at scale.

Event title: Nature data from the ground up: The 8 Billion Hour Pledge as a catalyst for global groundtruthing
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
Submitted timing preference: The first week of COP19 (i.e. Oct 19–24th), but we are open to considering later options.
List any other organizations, collaborat: Toha Network
Event description: Groundtruthing is a vital complement to earth observation data and other remote sensing technologies. It contributes scientific integrity and local nuance to high-granularity datasets. However, it also increases the cost of data and the need for community engagement, because in situ measurement interacts directly and visibly with place-based communities. This leaves a gap for intermediating infrastructure that brings together top-down and ground-up data collection at low cost, while also upholding the rights, trust and sovereignty of communities who live in the territories being measured. The 8 Billion Hour (8BH) Pledge addresses this gap by building a community-level verification layer that enables consent-based data collection and sharing. This serves the 8BH Pledge’s global campaign to register, verify and fund 8 billion hours of nature stewardship before 31 December 2030. But it also serves demand for groundtruthing data by creating an open marketplace where communities can deliver data collection and verification services. This event will introduce the 8BH Pledge and its digital infrastructure, the importance of community-level verification for FPIC and benefit-sharing, and articulate why groundtruthing is a critical complement for data reporting from NBSAPs to corporate disclosures.

Event title: From the Field to Structured Data: A Mobile App for Collecting and Integrating Biodiversity Data
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation
List any other organizations, collaborat: TaiBIF, Forestry and Conservation Agency
Event description:
Turning field observations into data that can inform policy takes far longer than collecting them: looking up species names, matching them to a checklist, confirming identifications, structuring the records, and reformatting everything to international standards. None of this is quick or easy, and much survey data never gets that far.
We developed Mitalivana, a mobile field app that integrates every step from collection to output. Users build species checklists, vegetation plots, animal surveys and specimen records, and export them structured in Darwin Core together with GBIF's survey and vegetation-plot vocabularies (the Humboldt and Relevé extensions). The same structured information is written into photo metadata, so images stay linked to their records. The app works fully offline for areas without signal (except map layers), and includes a framework for in-field identification keys. Country species lists downloaded from GBIF and iNaturalist, and it can also contribute back to iNaturalist. Our aim is to let citizen scientists, government agencies and professional surveyors collect more reliable data with less effort. Each field record then flows directly into species checklists, long-term monitoring, citizen-science platforms and global data infrastructure. Those sources underpin decisions and reporting under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Event title: From Space to Ground: Connecting Earth Observation with Real-Time Biodiversity Monitoring
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation
Submitted timing preference: Preference for the week of the 26th October
Event description:
Earth observation and remote sensing are transforming our ability to monitor biodiversity and ecosystem change at scale. However, translating these observations into actionable information also requires reliable, continuous evidence from the ground.
This session will explore how Green Box, a field-deployed environmental monitoring infrastructure, can complement satellite and remote-sensing systems by providing real-time and near-real-time observations directly from managed ecosystems. Combining autonomous sensors, connectivity and edge computing, Green Box can create a persistent link between what is observed remotely and what is happening on the ground, while reducing operational costs.
A key objective is to discuss how such infrastructure could support more standardized ground-truth observations, complementing initiatives led by GEO BON, GEO and other biodiversity monitoring networks and strengthening the validation and interpretation of Earth observation data.
The session will also examine the role of local communities as active participants in biodiversity monitoring, combining technology with local knowledge, field observations and stewardship (we can provide free internet connectivity, ...).
The central message is that effective biodiversity monitoring does not require choosing between satellites, field science or communities. Connecting these layers can create a more continuous, verifiable and locally relevant evidence system for biodiversity action.

Event title: Cambridge Sustainability Science Trends and Sustainable Finance Initiatives
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance
Event description:
The session opens with an overview of where sustainability science is currently moving: nature-related risk assessment, ecosystem condition accounting, double materiality, and the shift from carbon-only analysis toward nature-inclusive analysis. These are live methodological debates, not settled doctrine, and the presentation treats them as such.
It then narrows to sustainable finance, where the gap between ambition and evidence is widest. Financial institutions are being asked to assess nature-related risk across portfolios whose underlying borrowers produce no environmental data at all, and in many markets never will. The session sets out what the science says is genuinely measurable, what is not, where technology closes the gap, and, equally important, where it only appears to.
The closing argument is that the binding constraint on nature finance is no longer appetite or policy. It is the absence of evidence that survives an audit.

Event title: Turning Environmental DNA into Actionable Biodiversity Data: The PlutoF Monitoring and Publishing Workflow
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Submitted timing preference: after 20th of October, no other preference, according to thematic blocks
List any other organizations, collaborat: GBIF Estonia node
Event description:
Environmental DNA (eDNA) offers unprecedented opportunities to monitor biodiversity across terrestrial, freshwater, marine and agricultural ecosystems. This demonstration will present the end-to-end eDNA data pipeline developed within the PlutoF biodiversity data management platform, showing how biodiversity information is transformed from field samples into FAIR, policy-relevant data products. The workflow integrates sampling metadata, laboratory processing, DNA sequencing, bioinformatic analysis, taxonomic assignment using curated reference databases such as UNITE, and quality-controlled publication of results.
A key innovation is the conversion of eDNA-derived taxonomic detections into standardized biodiversity occurrence records that can be published through GBIF and reused in biodiversity assessments, monitoring programmes and Global Biodiversity Framework reporting. The pipeline supports interoperability through international biodiversity data standards and enables transparent data governance, provenance tracking and long-term accessibility.
The session will demonstrate how emerging molecular technologies can be connected with biodiversity observation infrastructures to address critical data gaps, improve biodiversity monitoring across ecosystems, and support evidence-based decision-making for conservation, business and One Health applications. By making eDNA data discoverable, accessible and reusable at global scale, PlutoF helps transform biodiversity observations into actionable knowledge for policy and society.

Event title: Counting nature: Biodiversity Measurement for tropical deployment at biome scale
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation
List any other organizations, collaborat: World Biodiversity Forum, University of Zurich,Business for Nature, Capitals Coalition, AI2, Conservation X-labs,  IPBES, GEO-BON
Event description:
Tropical forests hold more biodiversity than any other biome, yet they accounted for 94% of global deforestation during this century.  Therefore, building global economic and policy systems that make standing forests more valuable than cleared land is essential.  These systems must create tangible benefits for tropical countries, indigenous communities, local communities, and other forest stewards. 
This two panel session will examine how tropical forests can be measured, valued, and incorporated into financial and policy decisions.  Its objective is to identify practical pathways from translating scientific knowledge to credible, widely adopted systems that support forest conservation and sustainable development. 
The first panel will bring together leaders from science, policy, and business to explore which essential features of the complex forests ecosystems must be measured, monitored, and incorporated into financial systems.  Panelists will also discuss the barriers/challenges preventing shared frameworks from translating into effective action. 
The second panel will feature science and technology leaders advancing integrated monitoring systems.  They will discuss how new tools, common standards, and broad-scale adoption can support credible biodiversity valuation across sectors, and inform more effective decisions about the future of tropical forests.

Event title: From Monitoring to Reporting: Lessons and Perspectives from Transnational, Subregional and National Monitoring Initiatives
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: Biodiversa +, Syke, OFB, European Commission DG Research & Innovation, European Commission JRC, Instituto Humboldt, INRAE, OSS, UNEP-WCMC, German National Monitoring Centre for Biodiversity
Event description:
One barrier to successful implementation of the GBF2030 is the mismatch between global and national indicator reporting. With a few years left to achieve these goals and a timely half-term review, this event will discuss: How can transnational monitoring contribute to CBD reporting?
In this event, we are bringing together representatives from the three scales of reporting, from national, regional, and global perspectives, to share their experiences and shed light on successes, challenges, and synergies. The 1.5-hour session brings together five speakers from different institutions and roles: UNEP WCMC, Biodiversa+, the German National Monitoring Centre for Biodiversity, and three TSCC regions, including the European Commission Knowledge Centre for Biodiversity (KCBD), the Humboldt Foundation, and the Observatory of the Sahara and the Sahel (OSS).
The discussion will explore how monitoring systems at transnational, subregional and national levels can be better connected, how experiences and approaches can be shared across scales, and how these efforts can contribute to effective CBD reporting and implementation. 
The session will be open to the audience, providing an opportunity for participants to share experiences, raise questions, and engage in an open exchange on opportunities and challenges for strengthening biodiversity monitoring and reporting across scales.

Event title: Women in Technology for Sustainability
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation
Event description:
This is not a panel about representation. It is a showcase of working technology, presented by the women who built it.
An award-winning woman founders with Armenian origins present a live environmental or sustainability technology: the problem it measures, how the system works, and what it took to build in a small market with a thin capital base. A short moderated segment follows on building deep technology outside the major innovation hubs, and the session closes with open questions.
The emphasis throughout is on method and engineering rather than on founder narrative. Attendees should leave knowing how several environmental measurement tools actually function, and who to contact to use them.

Event title: Youth for Biodiversity: Connecting Knowledge Systems for Collective Action
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: GEO BON
Event description:
Earth observation has transformed our ability to see the planet. But what we choose to observe, and who decides what counts as evidence, remains a socially embedded question. As Parties move from global review to national implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF), this session frames the gap between data and action not only as technical, but also as a gap between knowledge systems: between satellite imagery and the place-based expertise of Indigenous Peoples and local communities; between the natural sciences that build indicators and the social sciences that explain how decisions are made; and between the institutions that hold data and the generations who will live with its consequences.

This session aims to test a simple hypothesis: new solutions for implementation emerge from new ways of observing. It aims to bring together young researchers and practitioners, Indigenous and local knowledge holders, Earth observation specialists, policymakers and social scientists for a cross-sectoral conversation on how to widen what counts as “observable,” who gets to observe it, and why.

The discussion is organised around four entry points: 
1.	Knowledge systems as infrastructure. Indigenous and local knowledge is not a supplement to monitoring. It is a way of observing ecosystems in its own right, with its own methods, continuity and authority, as recognised in KMGBF Targets 21 and 22. 
2.	Rights of “Nature.” The KMGBF acknowledges diverse value systems, including, for countries that recognise them, the rights of nature and of Mother Earth. What would it mean for monitoring to track not only ecosystem extent and condition, but whether nature’s standing is respected? And, ultimately, define what is “nature” and what rights does it hold? 
3.	Youth as a standpoint. Young people are often consulted, but unfortunately rarely heard. The session treats youth as a legitimate and credible perspective: those who will inherit the 2030 and 2050 outcomes are best placed to ask whether today’s tools are fit for them. 
4.	Interdisciplinarity for implementation. Translating global targets into local action requires the social sciences inside the technical work: understanding governance, power, language, and context so that data can move decisions. 

The session is designed as an open, facilitated exchange. The result of this session will prompt GEO’s next action on youth engagement and participation.
Key Messages:
-	Observation is never neutral. Deciding what is “observable” is a choice about whose knowledge counts. Widening that choice is a precondition for effective monitoring.
-	Plural knowledge systems strengthen the evidence base. Indigenous and local knowledge, EO and field science answer different questions. Implementation needs all of them, on equal terms.
-	Youth hold standing, as essential stakeholders and agents of change, not a symbolic seat at the table. As the generation that will live with the outcomes of the 2050 Vision, young people bring an innovative, long-term perspective on whether current tools serve lasting outcomes, and should be engaged at every stage, from design to implementation and review.
-	The data-to-action gap is social as much as technical. Integrating the social sciences early is how global targets become locally meaningful and politically actionable.
-	The main challenge lies in implementation. Much of what's needed in terms of solutions already exists. The task is to connect it across sectors and generations.

Event title: A Single Framework for Prior Informed Consent for Digital Sequence Information
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: Amber Scholz, senior Access and Benefit-Sharing policy expert and microbiologist, Leibniz Institute DSMZ
Event description: This session will discuss the potential advantages from standardized methodologies to accomplish compliance with Nagoya Protocol Access and Benefits Sharing (ABS), and introduces a single standardized framework for prior informed consent governing Digital Sequence Information (DSI). Modeled on the concept of the Simple Agreement for Future Equity (SAFE) that transformed early-stage startup investment, the framework delivers one interoperable set of terms that a provider and a sovereign rights holder can execute quickly and predictably, replacing the need for individualized bilateral negotiations. By reducing legal and policy complexities that can delay or deter data sharing, the approach addresses core challenges of data governance and facilitates the practical implementation of DSI projects. It is designed to promote both bilateral ABS benefit flows and contributions to multilateral mechanisms such as the Cali Fund, ensuring that sequence data is shared under appropriately governed, transparent, and verifiable procedures that support the Nagoya Protocol and the broader international policy architecture of the Convention on Biological Diversity. Because a common framework must work across sectors and stakeholder groups, the session is intended for a diverse CBD audience, including academic researchers, public database and sequence-repository stewards, industry users, providers and Indigenous Peoples and local communities. Participants will be invited to test the model against their respective needs, legal and policy contexts, and practical experience. The session will bring together perspectives  from database holders, policy experts, and the private sector, and will encourage active audience participation and a robust question-and-answer discussion throughout. The goal is to critically test the proposed framework and associated tools and work toward a practical and effective approach that can serve a range of DSI governance contexts.

Lead organization: Group on Earth Observation, Global Ecosystems Atlas
Event title: Bridging Public-Private Data to Accelerate Biodiversity Action
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: UNEP-WCMC, CDP
Event description:
COP17 will set the stage for the first, comprehensive Global Review – a critical litmus test of collective progress of action for biodiversity. The IPBES Business and Biodiversity Assessment, published in early 2026, affirmed that all businesses depend on and impact biodiversity and can be agents of positive change. This is recognized in the Target 15 of the KMGBF, and the positioning of the KMGBF as a whole-of-society framework. 
The IPBES Business and Biodiversity Assessment also highlighted that while there already is sufficient data for businesses to start taking action on biodiversity, many data gaps remain. How can public data on biodiversity become more accessible for business use? And how does corporate information in turn help implement and monitor countries' progress on NBSAPs? 
This event will showcase case studies of successful data collaborations between public and private sector, which are helping to accelerate progress on NBSAP implementation and support the private sector with trusted, high quality data on ecosystems and species. Global Ecosystems Atlas, GBIF and CDP will share lessons from building pioneering collaborations on data. A panel discussion on benefits of breaking the data silos between public and private sector will bring together speakers from the Government of Japan (TBC) and UK (TBC), private sector (speakers TBC) and research (speakers TBC).

Event title: Unlocking Deal Flow: Aligning supply-side/demand-side data and assurance for the emerging biodiversity markets
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: Deloitte Global, and the Biodiversity Credit Alliance
Event description:
The emerging biodiversity markets present a potential financing tool to help bridge the ~$800b annual global biodiversity financing gap through innovative private sector financing. Without consolidated demand from corporate buyers this market will stagnate. 
Demand barriers include corporate hesitancy to commit funds at scale in the face of uncertainty and potential reputational risk in an emerging market. The spectrum of potential corporate nature-related claim types, emerging corporate nature standards and associated mitigation hierarchy, data and assurance requirements adds to this uncertainty.
This workshop targets a) demand-side actors to share insights into their priorities, data and assurance requirements, and b) supply-side actors seeking to integrate their MRV data and assurance frameworks with these demand-side imperatives. The underlying purpose is to make a contribution to towards unlocking market deal flow at scale.

Event title: GEO-Wetlands: Operationalizing Wetland Earth Observation for National Action and KMGBF Reporting
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: European Space Agency, Ramsar Convention on Wetlands Secretariat, DHI
Event description:
Inland and coastal wetlands are vital to achieving Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) Targets 1, 2, and 3, alongside the Convention on Wetlands 5th Strategic Plan (SP5). Yet, Parties continually face fragmented baselines and technical bottlenecks when monitoring wetland extent and ecological condition.
Convened by GEO-Wetlands and aligned with the Ramsar STRP work programme, this session delivers an operational roadmap to embed Earth Observation (EO) directly into national policy and reporting. By moving past isolated pilots to institutionalized monitoring, the session links EO capabilities to the Ramsar Secretariat’s Wetland Inventory Guidance.
Central to this transition are Essential Wetland Variables (EWVs). Standardizing metrics for extent, hydrology, and condition establishes credible, shared benchmarks. This harmonization bridges national inventories with international reporting under both the CBD and the Convention on Wetlands.
Global Mangrove Watch (GMW) serves as a mature proof of concept for this end-to-end value chain. It demonstrates how multi-sensor satellite imagery converts into high-resolution annual extents, near-real-time disturbance alerts, and verified carbon accounting, data ministries already rely on for spatial planning, protected area enforcement, and official treaty submissions. Finally, the session highlights scaling these standardized workflows across all wetland realms via emerging platforms like Global Wetland Watch and the Wetland Atlas, equipping Parties with the unified tools needed to track conservation targets at scale.

Lead organization: Sustainable Forestry Initiative's Project Learning Tree
Event title: Forests to Faucets: Environmental Education Tools using GIS Data Exploration for all ages
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Submitted timing preference: October 21 afternoon; October 23 afternoon; October 26th anytime
List any other organizations, collaborat: Esri
Event description:
Achieving the goals of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework requires expanding access to scientific knowledge, digital tools, and capacity-building opportunities that empower learners and educators to understand and address biodiversity challenges. Aligned with Target 20, this interactive session demonstrates how freely accessible geospatial technologies can strengthen environmental education while fostering scientific and technical cooperation across educational communities. 
Participants will explore hands-on lessons designed by Sustainable Forest Initiative’s Project Learning Tree to engage young people in investigating the interconnected relationships among forests, watersheds, biodiversity, and drinking water quality using the Forests to Faucets 2.0 GIS Data Explorer, a free tool developed on Esri ArcGIS technology and maintained by the USDA Forest Service. Through real-world geospatial inquiry, learners can identify the sources of their drinking water, analyze potential environmental threats, and develop a systems-based understanding of ecosystem services and natural resource stewardship.
 The session will provide an overview of each lesson, its learning objectives, and academic standards alignment, followed by a demonstration of the GIS platform and its classroom applications.

Lead organization: Group on Earth Observations, Global Ecosystems Atlas
Event title: Leveraging nature data for assurable corporate disclosures
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: TNFD, UNEP-WCMC
Event description: Improving the availability and accessibility of biodiversity data for business is an important catalyst to scale the number of companies monitoring, disclosing and taking action on biodiversity. Providers and aggregators of biodiversity data for private sector use need clarity on requirements that data needs to meet to effectively support business users and their disclosures. In 2025, TNFD published a first version of their Nature Data Principles for state of nature data used in corporate assessments and disclosure, building on existing data principles such as FAIR, CARE, Open Data Charter or TDWG for GBIF. This session will convene a discussion on opportunities and challenges in building a consensus on a common set of principles for biodiversity data used by the private sector, and how this could support progress on the KMGBF Target 15. Across two panel discussions, speakers will include data providers (e.g. GEO, GBIF (TBC), IUCN (TBC), UNEP-WCMC), TNFD, as well as representatives of business data users, data aggregators and custodians of biodiversity data from Indigenous Peoples and other local communities.

Event title: GEO-TREES as global infrastructure for valuing forests: Establishing a rigorous ground-validation system for valuing forests – from carbon to biodiversity - at scale.
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
List any other organizations, collaborat: Government of Panama, Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation, European Space Agency, ETHZ.
Event description:
Tropical forests hold more biodiversity than any other biome on the planet, and yet 94% of the deforestation in this century took place in the tropics. It is vital that we build global structures that will allow all tropical countries, and tropical forest landholders to generate more value from standing forests than from cleared land.  
Developed through a collaboration involving hundreds of scientific organizations worldwide, GEO-TREES is establishing large-scale calibration and validation sites across tropical forest types  and conditions.  These sites will provide the essential data to accurately value forests at scale.  Although, GEO-TREES addresses both carbon and biodiversity, its initial goal is to establish a robust, dynamic global inventory of carbon – at project relevant scales – for the world’s tropical forests.  
Through two panel discussions, this session will introduce GEO-TREES, – the ambition, the science, the potential impact on its capacity to value forests within traditional market structures.  
The first panel will introduce the project, explore the science objectives, and outline the global impacts of counting carbon, and establishing global infrastructure for forest biodiversity monitoring.  The second panel will bring together policymakers, philanthropy, and market participants to explore how trusted data and shared standards can reduce risk in biodiversity markets, improve project-level carbon accounting, and increase investment in topical forests.

Event title: How to use Earth observation (EO) for genetic diversity monitoring
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Submitted timing preference: Monday Oct 26, preferably 12:30 (EN) with additional slot at 10:00 (ES)
List any other organizations, collaborat: GEO BON, GBIF, ESA, Coalition for Conservation Genetics; current test cases in Australia, Namibia, Slovenia, South Korea, South Africa, USA, Nepal, Kenya, Norway, Sweden, Zambia, Tanzania
Event description: Genetic diversity within and among populations is essential for species persistence, yet challenging to measure at country and regional scales. Parties to the CBD require reliable and efficient assessments of genetic diversity at the country scale (Headline Indicator A.4). We will explain how space-based Earth observation (EO) can compliment field measurements helping to monitor the GBF genetic diversity indicators at the country scale. We will showcase a stepwise, free, public and open workflow that makes EO accessible for this purpose, and show how this workflow can enable reporting on genetic diversity indicators and empower progress towards the GBF. We will then have open discussions about opportunities and challenges for this approach in light of reporting experiences with target A.4 in the first global reporting period, and implementing the presented workflow for the upcoming reporting period in 2029. The format will be a 30-minute on-stage presentation and demo followed by a 10-minute on-stage Q&A and 20-minute small-group mingle and exchange. Catering will be provided.

Event title: From Data Consumption to Circulation: Co-Creating Biodiversity Data Ecosystems with the Business Sector
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
List any other organizations, collaborat: Toyota Motor Corporation
Event description: As the global transition towards a nature-positive future accelerates, corporate decisions regarding land-use and economic activities carry unprecedented significance for biodiversity outcomes. Translating commitments into effective action requires robust, science-based biodiversity assessments. Amid persistent global data gaps and spatial bias, the business sector—routinely generating primary observation data through its operations—represents a crucial player for enriching the global biodiversity data infrastructure. Drawing on pioneering experience in Japan, this session presents a transformative data circulation model to clean, standardize, and integrate dormant corporate data into global repositories in accordance with rigorous scientific protocols. Moving beyond one-off data consumption, this framework empowers companies to transition from passive data users into active contributors to the global knowledge base. By anchoring corporate decision-making in reliable evidence while simultaneously addressing critical knowledge gaps, speakers will outline an actionable roadmap for co-creating an inclusive biodiversity data ecosystem that advances the targets of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Event title: Nature-based Education Learning Portal, PANORAMA and IUCN Academy - How to Integrate Initiatives to Develop Knowledge Systems
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Submitted timing preference: 27 October, preferrably in the morning or early afternoon
Event description:
As biodiversity loss accelerates, educators, governments, youth, and communities urgently need better tools to learn about, with, and for nature. This session will introduce three initiatives led by IUCN and showcase how they form the basis for an integrated approach to generate knowledge systems for people.
The NbE Learning Portal is being developed by IUCN and its Commission on Education and Communication together with Esri. It showcases geospatial tools for nature education -biodiversity, climate, water, land, and more and maps NbE activity worldwide, surfacing shared lessons, and providing ArcGIS-based tools to educators, students, and civil society.
PANORAMA – Solutions for a Healthy Planet brings the practitioner knowledge component to this integrated approach. Through a global repository of proven conservation and sustainable development solutions, it enables peer learning by capturing lessons from the field and organising them into adaptable “building blocks” for replication.
Finally, the IUCN Academy brings the training and capacity building component to the approach. It harnesses the Union’s expertise to build capacity around skills and tools required to protect nature and promote sustainability. It helps scale the reach and impact of lessons and recommendations from complementary knowledge systems, including PANORAMA experiences and NbE approaches.

Lead organization: UK Centre for Ecology and hydrology
Event title: Ensuring Equitable Biodiversity Monitoring in LMICs: Technology and Data Pathways to Advance KMGBF Implementation
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
Event description: This event will present and discuss the findings from the UK Government funded Innovate 4 Nature programme, which has identified future opportunities for biodiversity monitoring technologies and data outputs, the interconnected barriers impacting access and adoption across low- and middle-income countries, and how to best facilitate technology and knowledge transfer, ensuring technology is accessible and equitable, and that data is accessible relevant and utilised in decision making

Event title: Business biodiversity data. How can companies contribute to the monitoring and implementation of the KMGBF?
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
List any other organizations, collaborat: IRD (France) SiB Colombia . Humboldt Institute (Colombia) ANDI (Colombia)
Event description:
Economic activities and business operations generate large biodiversity datasets, in particular through impact assessment processes. In a context where data is a key driver of ecological transformation, and where private organizations are themselves becoming data producers, it is crucial to safeguard and share this knowledge to monitor biodiversity status and trends and inform progress towards global biodiversity targets set by KMGBF. This event will present the legal frameworks established by France and Colombia which mandate to deliver such data to public information systems, as well as from the institutions that manage these dataflows, and the network of buisness that produce them. Several common challenges will be adressed : quality, attribution of authorship, processing time, compliance, the effectiveness of obligations, and other data uses such as TNFD. Other discussion topic will focus at major forest basins where massive dataflows are generated by companies for certification purposes without a clear and harmonized process for publication and accessibility. 
The event will foster a public-private dialogue to explore how to work together, particularly by drawing on research to develop recognized methods that private organizations can use to conduct more effective impact assessments and sustainability. This will be illustrated by the DeepForestVision and DeepForestSound tools (One Forest Vision initiative), which bring new possibilities for facilitating qualitative assessments of the impact of human activities on animal biodiversity.
Speakers will include representatives of public institutions, business sectors, and local stakeholders and communities.

Event title: Building the Global Biodiversity Observing System: GEO BON’s global biodiversity network
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: ESA, UNEP-WCMC, SANBI, RCMRD
Event description:
Four years into implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, countries need biodiversity monitoring systems that can turn observations into information for indicators, reporting and decision-making. GEO BON is working with its global network of national, regional and thematic Biodiversity Observation Networks (BONs), Essential Biodiversity Variable (EBV) communities, partners and technical initiatives to help build this capacity.
This session will provide an update on how GEO BON is translating the vision of a Global Biodiversity Observing System (GBiOS) into practical action. It will highlight progress across the network, including the development and strengthening of BONs; advances in EBVs and indicators; BON in a Box and reproducible data-to-decision workflows; emerging areas such as animal movement and One Health; and partnerships connecting Earth observation, biodiversity data, technology and national monitoring.
We look ahead to the next phase of implementation: how these pieces can work together as a more connected global observing system that strengthens national biodiversity monitoring while contributing to regional and global understanding of biodiversity change.
Through short presentations and discussion with GEO BON members and partners, the session will explore what is already working, where important gaps remain, and where collaboration and investment can accelerate the transition from biodiversity observations to sustained monitoring and action.

Lead organization: Group on Earth Observations, Global Ecosystems Atlas
Event title: From Ecosystem Intelligence to Action: Using Ecosystem Data to Identify Risk and Prioritise Resilience Investments in Insurance and Banking
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
Submitted timing preference: Tuesday 27th approx 2pm or the afternoon of Thurs 22nd but we can be flexible
List any other organizations, collaborat: UNEP-FI, Aviva
Event description:
Financial institutions increasingly recognise that nature loss and climate change are interconnected drivers of physical risk. However, understanding where risks occur is only the first step. To make effective investment, financing and insurance decisions, organisations also need to understand the ecosystems that underpin resilience and provide critical services such as flood regulation, water security and climate adaptation. 

This session will explore how ecosystem extent data can be combined to integrate nature insights into climate risk modelling to drive better decision-making across banking, insurance and investment portfolios. Bringing together leaders from finance, data platforms and nature science, the discussion will examine how improved ecosystem information can strengthen physical risk assessments, reveal the value of ecosystem services from different ecosystems, and help identify and prioritise investments in nature-based solutions. 

Through practical examples, including efforts to model and then reduce flood risk through landscape-scale nature restoration, speakers will demonstrate how translating biodiversity and ecosystem data into actionable insights can help move from risk identification to real-world resilience outcomes. 

The session will highlight the growing role of ecosystem data in supporting risk management, investment decisions and progress towards global biodiversity and climate goals, while addressing broader challenges around data availability, usability and decision relevance.

Event title: From Knowledge to Action: Connecting Communities, Indigenous Knowledge, and Biodiversity Science Through Place
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
List any other organizations, collaborat: Jane Goodall Institute (confirmed) , Amazon Conservation Team (likely), Cadasta Foundation (potential)
Event description: Conservation succeeds through relationships: relationships between people and nature, between knowledge systems, and between communities working toward a shared future. Geography provides a common language for understanding and connecting these relationships across cultures, disciplines, and scales. Achieving the goals of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework requires connecting diverse knowledge systems, empowering people with access to biodiversity information, and ensuring the meaningful participation of Indigenous Peoples and local communities in decisions affecting biodiversity. Drawing on real-world conservation initiatives from around the world, speakers will share experiences applying geographic information systems (GIS) to connect knowledge systems, strengthen participation, and support community stewardship. Attendees will learn how GIS unites traditional knowledge, local observations, and biodiversity science to empower communities to participate in decision-making and translate knowledge into action for biodiversity.

Event title: From Mapping to Management: Geospatial Solutions for Protected Areas
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
List any other organizations, collaborat: Wildlife Conservation Society, Frankfurt Zoological Society, others (SERCA?)
Event description:
Geospatial technologies are rapidly changing how we understand the world—and creating new possibilities for how we protect it. Across landscapes and seascapes, we have the opportunity to transform protected areas management by equipping the people responsible for conservation with real-time data, easy-to-use tools, and powerful place-based analytics to drive informed and coordinated action. 
This session will explore how innovation in geospatial technologies empowers field observations, Earth observation, AI, spatial analysis, and operational workflows—from daily protected area management and biodiversity monitoring to strategic planning, reporting, and measuring impact. It will showcase GIS (geographic information systems) as a unifying framework that brings together people, data, technologies, and knowledge to strengthen coordination and translate monitoring and innovation into conservation action. There will be a demonstration of the new release of ArcGIS for Protected Areas Management, real-world lessons from organizations doing this work, and pathways to access, learn, and effectively apply these technologies, building the capacity to put innovation into practice.

Event title: Biodiversity in motion: New approaches for incorporating animal movement observations into policy and practice
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: Francesca Cagnacci, Fondazione Edmund Mach,   President International Biologging Society; Thomas Müller, Senckenberg
Event description:
Advances in animal tracking technologies now allow researchers to monitor animal movement, behavior, physiology, and survival. Yet, these data remain largely disconnected from the global frameworks guiding conservation and sustainable development. The Animal Movement Biodiversity Observation Network (Move BON) is closing this gap by engaging a global community to mobilize animal movement data and generate policy-relevant insights. This session will highlight advances in expanding data mobilization and improved metrics and indicators measuring the processes driving biodiversity change. Proposed topics include:  
WildMoves, a new GBIF-hosted data portal featuring animal tracking data sets that meet the rigorous standards required for global-scale analysis of biodiversity datasets.   
MoveTraits, a new database of standardized movement metrics calculated from animal tracking data. MoveTraits aims to make behavioral information contained in biologging data more accessible, supporting trait-based change detection.  
A new Diurnality Indicator linking animal behavior with human activities, tracking behavioral responses to rapid environmental change and supporting proactive conservation under the GBF. 
The Global Animal Mortality Project, uses tracking data to reveal the mechanisms of species loss at a global scale. As part of this project, we are developing a new mortality-based biodiversity indicator to monitoring of the processes driving population change.

Lead organization: (RCMRD) Regional Centre for Mapping of Resources for Development
Event title: From Outlook to Action: Translating the Eastern and Southern Africa Biodiversity Assessment into KMGBF Progress
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
Submitted timing preference: Tuesday, 27 October 2026, between 11:00 AM and 1:00 PM. We would prefer a slot in the second week if possible, ideally within this window.
List any other organizations, collaborat: Lead organization: RCMRD (Regional Centre for Mapping of Resources for Development), under the Regional Centre of Excellence (RCoE) Project. Event description: This session presents key findings from the newly developed Biodiversity and Ecosystems Outlook for Eastern and Southern Africa (BOESA), a regional publication mapping the state of biodiversity, ecosystem services, and the policies that govern them across 24 countries. The talk focuses on gaps the assessment uncovered in how biodiversity data is collected, shared, and used for decision-making: data that stays siloed within institutions and often with individuals rather than the institutions themselves due to limited trust; the absence of shared standards, which makes it hard to compare data across agencies; duplicated data-collection efforts that waste resources and produce conflicting figures; delays in harmonizing scattered datasets that push national reports to the CBD past deadline; and weak or missing legal frameworks for data-sharing. Drawing on complementary work from the Regional Centre of Excellence's policy briefs on biodiversity data governance, the session will connect these findings to concrete recommendations for turning fragmented data into decisions including how countries can strengthen data-sharing frameworks, close reporting gaps, and make monitoring systems more inclusive. The goal is to give participants a clear, practical picture of where Eastern and Southern Africa stands on biodiversity data readiness, and what needs to happen next to support countries in tracking and reporting progress under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The session closes with an open floor for questions and potential collaboration.

Event title: Where will action count most? Calibrating global data with local knowledge
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
Submitted timing preference: Flexible, we have four IBAT staff attending the event and should be able to cover most slots. We would be glad to pick from a set of available slots once the programme takes shape.
List any other organizations, collaborat: IUCN
Event description:
The IUCN RHINO (Rapid High-Integrity Nature-positive Outcomes) approach helps companies, governments and civil society understand what to do, where to act, and how to measure progress. It offers a ready-to-implement, robust route for those with control over sites, supply chains and investments to deliver Nature Positive outcomes, and to contribute measurably to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Its core metric is STAR, the Species Threat Abatement and Restoration metric, derived from the IUCN Red List of Threatened Species. Following the TNFD LEAP framework, RHINO takes a user from locating sensitive areas, to confirming which species and threats are genuinely present and defining a baseline, to prioritising threats, setting targets, delivering action, and reporting what was achieved.
This session walks through key steps with an illustrative case study, then focuses on the one that joins global data to local reality: calibration. The starting point is an IBAT Species Report, the species and threats expected at a site, which is then checked against what data gathered on the ground show. Attendees will try calibrating a site themselves, using the tool now available through IBAT (Integrated Biodiversity Assessment Tool).

Event title: Connecting networks, data and decisions through a GBIF-GEO BON partnership
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: GBIF, Colombia, New Zealand
Event description:
How can stronger connections between biodiversity data infrastructure and observation networks support action for nature? Join GEO BON and the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) at the Data to Action Pavilion to explore their complementary roles and celebrate the signing of a Memorandum of Cooperation.
GBIF’s global network of nodes and publishers mobilizes and shares biodiversity data through common standards and open infrastructure. GEO BON advances coordinated biodiversity observations, the Essential Biodiversity Variables framework, and tools to support monitoring and indicator development. Together, the networks can strengthen the connections between data availability, scientific analysis and policy needs.
The event will feature introductions to both networks and perspectives from GBIF nodes and Biodiversity Observation Networks on opportunities for collaboration. A practical BON in a Box demonstration will illustrate how mobilized biodiversity data can support analysis and monitoring, and how a new approach allows querying cloud-optimized biodiversity data structured through the Darwin Core Data Package.
The session will conclude with the MOC signing and a discussion of future joint activities, including capacity development, identifying and addressing data gaps, and supporting implementation of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. Researchers, data holders, practitioners and policymakers are invited to discover opportunities to participate.

Event title: Nature Footprint: Nature-related Life Cycle Assessment method for advancing Business and Financial Action
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
Submitted timing preference: October 27, 2026, 9:00 AM–3:00 PM, or October 28, 2026, 9:00 AM–5:00 PM (local time in Yerevan)
Event description:
Biodiversity data provide an essential foundation for understanding changes in nature, but translating scientific knowledge into actionable information for businesses and financial institutions remains a key challenge. Nature Footprint is a science-based approach that connects biodiversity data and impact assessment with practical decision-making. This event will demonstrate how biodiversity knowledge can move from data to assessment and ultimately to action.
The session will begin with an overview of the Nature Footprint concept and its role in measuring and communicating biodiversity impacts. It will then introduce a spatially explicit approach for assessing the impacts of land-use change on biodiversity, showing how biodiversity data and differences across locations can be translated into quantitative impact information. Finally, the session will present the application of Nature Footprint to financial institutions, illustrating how biodiversity footprint information can support the assessment of financial activities and portfolios.
By connecting biodiversity data, scientific assessment, and practical applications, the event aims to demonstrate a pathway from biodiversity data to action. It will show how Nature Footprint can translate biodiversity knowledge into actionable information for business and financial decision-making, while contributing to the implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Event title: Indicator T6.1 on Invasive Alien Species
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
List any other organizations, collaborat: GBIF, Australia, Monash Univesity
Event description: How can countries use biodiversity data to track progress in preventing biological invasions? This event introduces Headline Indicator 6.1, the rate of invasive alien species establishment, and its role in monitoring Target 6 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework. The session will explain the indicator’s methodology and the data needed to calculate it: national checklists of invasive alien species, information on when species established, and estimates of survey effort over time. It will explore how national information can complement open resources, including the Global Register of Introduced and Invasive Species, the First Records database and species occurrence data available through GBIF. Drawing on country examples, the session will examine how to interpret establishment trends, assess data completeness and understand what the results mean for progress towards Target 6. Participants will also learn about a calculation pipeline under development to help countries use their own data alongside open sources. The discussion will highlight opportunities to strengthen national monitoring and data sharing to support prevention, management and reporting.

Event title: Practical application of science-based biodiversity tools for the private sector: ENCORE, IBAT and the Nature Tools Compass
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Event description:
As businesses and financial institutions increasingly take steps to understand and manage their nature dependencies, impacts, risks and opportunities, lessons are emerging on how to implement this in practice: where to begin, which tools to use, and how to interpret the outputs to inform decision-making and support implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework and its monitoring framework.
This showcase will dive into leading nature tools developed by conservation organisations - ENCORE, IBAT and the Nature Tools Compass - before highlighting actionable business insights and inviting participants to explore practical application.

Event title: Wildlife Conservation Translocations: Bridging Species Recovery, Ecosystem Restoration, and One Health
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: IUCN SSC Conservation Translocation Specialist Group,   Panthera,   WWF International,   IUCN Forest and Grasslands Team,   Born Free Foundation,   VetMedUni Vienna,   Wildlife Conservation Society,   World Organisation for Animal Health,    World Federation for Animals
Event description:
Conservation translocations—including reintroductions, reinforcements, assisted colonization, and ecological replacements—are increasingly used to prevent extinctions, recover species, restore ecosystems, and support landscape connectivity under the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), contributing to species recovery under Target 4, ecosystem restoration under Target 2, and broader sustainable wildlife management efforts under Target 5. 
However, monitoring and implementation frameworks have not evolved at the same pace. Important gaps remain in tracking the implementation and long-term outcomes of conservation translocations and associated restoration efforts across ecological, health, genetic, welfare, spatial, and socio-economic dimensions. Existing guidance provides important foundations, yet monitoring frameworks, indicators, reporting systems, and best practices remain fragmented across regions and sectors. 
Building on discussions initiated at COP16, this panel will bring together scientists, policymakers, conservation practitioners, wildlife health experts, intergovernmental organizations, and civil society to discuss gaps, needs, and opportunities for improving the implementation and monitoring of conservation translocations under the GBF. Discussions will explore the need for integrated monitoring frameworks, post-release monitoring, adaptive management, indicators, and best practices, alongside emerging science-policy initiatives and examples from Kenya and other regions, while considering opportunities for knowledge exchange and coordination across sectors and regions.

Event title: CEOS Biodiversity Virtual Constellation: leveraging satellite Earth Observations for global biodiversity
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Submitted timing preference: Any date from Thursday 22 October and Thursday 29 October
List any other organizations, collaborat: GEO BON, Secretariat of the Convention on Wetlands, Country
Event description: The implementation of the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework requires timely, consistent and scientifically robust information to support evidence-based decision-making, monitor progress towards the GBF Goals and Targets, and strengthen the implementation of NBSAPs. Satellite Earth Observation provides unprecedented capabilities to monitor ecosystems, habitats and environmental change consistently across local, national and global scales. The Committee on Earth Observation Satellites (CEOS) plays a key role in coordinating civil space-based EO programmes internationally, helping to ensure that satellite observations and derived information deliver societal benefits and support sustainable decision-making. Through its Virtual Constellations, CEOS coordinates satellite observations, data products and related systems to address specific societal challenges. In April 2026, CEOS established the Biodiversity Virtual Constellation (B-VC) to strengthen the contribution and use of space-based EO for biodiversity understanding, monitoring and decision-making. This event will introduce the new CEOS B-VC and its activities, structured around six main pillars: (1) identifying priority gaps in observations and data products and facilitating solutions to address them; (2) enhancing data processing and utilisation tools to broaden the use of EO for biodiversity applications; (3) exploring prototype monitoring systems to support the development and testing of EO products; (4) implementing capacity-building activities; (5) strengthening engagement between the biodiversity and EO communities; and (6) coordinating with GEO BON and its Global Biodiversity Observing System concept to facilitate the wider use of space-based EO. The event will combine a presentation of the CEOS B-VC with an interactive panel discussion bringing together key stakeholders from the scientific, policy, institutional and user communities, including GEO BON, the Convention on Wetlands, TNFD and country representatives. The discussion will explore priority biodiversity monitoring needs, opportunities for greater uptake of satellite EO, and how international coordination can help translate EO capabilities into actionable information supporting GBF implementation.

Event title: From knowledge to action : empowering knowledge holders to engage in environmental and science-policy processes (CBD, IPBES, IPCC)
Paired thematic focus: Data Gaps & Governance + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
Submitted timing preference: Second week of the COP - everyday - 13:15 or 18:15
List any other organizations, collaborat: French MoE, CBD Secretariat, CO-OP4CBD, BioAgora, Biodiversa+, RESPIN, Norwegian Institute for Nature Research
Event description:
Open-access online learning tools (courses, toolkit, factsheets) are key to make complex environmental governance processes more accessible and actionable for a wide range of stakeholders. Effective biodiversity governance, including national monitoring and data reporting by local communities and biodiversity-policies’ practitioners, implies to strengthen their ability to contribute to global environmental processes.
A key objective of this side event is to ensure that key resources produced to engage in the CBD and in SPI processes, including IPBES and IPCC, are available not only to different categories of actors, but also across countries and regions, including those where English, Spanish and French are shared working languages for international engagement. As reflected in the agenda for COP17, capacity-building remains a key component of discussions on implementation (Item 12.a) and is structuring to achieve a whole-of-society approach.
Our event will bring together regional initiatives developing capacity-building activities to engage with the CBD, IPBES and IPCC. It will feature engagement strategies, methods and tools to include IPLCs in Science-Policy-Practice interfaces as well as specific open access tools to bridge Science and Policy, both in the CBD and in Rio-Conventions’ related intergovernmental platforms such as IPBES and IPCC.

Event title: From Complex to Compelling - How science reaches heads of state and hearts of the people
Paired thematic focus: Connecting Knowledge Systems & People + Building Capacity for Biodiversity Action
List any other organizations, collaborat: World Biodiversity Forum, University of Zurich
Event description:
Let’s Feel the Facts
How science and art can make data reach heads of state and the hearts of people.
How we communicate data is dated. Every body of research shows that facts don’t move people; emotions do. To turn our spreadsheets into full streets, we need to learn to find the emotions in data and bring them alive.
In collaboration with the World Biodiversity Forum, artist and science communicator Thijs Biersteker will take us on a journey from creating blockbuster art shows that make trees speak about climate change to being at the heart of the World Economic Forum, where heads of state walked under a data visualisation about deforestation every day.
The groundbreaking art x science communication work he does with his team at WOVEN is reshaping how dry data moves people, stakeholders, boardrooms and conferences, like the major work on invasive species here at COP17.

Event title: From Observation to Action: Using Open Biodiversity Data for Early Detection of Invasive Alien Plants
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
Submitted timing preference: Flexible, except for 19-21 Oct, which is when I will be showcasing SWAT at the Expo.
Event description:
Invasive alien species are a major driver of biodiversity loss worldwide, yet new incursions are often not detected until they have become widespread and difficult to manage. This event will showcase the Smart Weed Alert Tool (SWAT), an innovative system that helps identify potential new invasive plant species at the earliest stages of establishment.
SWAT automatically scans biodiversity observations shared through the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), including records contributed by citizen scientists through platforms such as iNaturalist. The system analyses these data and generates alerts when unusual or potentially invasive plant species are recorded in a particular area.
Through a live demonstration, participants will see how biodiversity observations can be transformed into practical decision-support tools that support rapid action. The session will illustrate how citizen science, open biodiversity data, and digital innovation can work together to strengthen biosecurity and biodiversity conservation.
Key messages are that biodiversity data can generate real-world conservation outcomes, that early detection is critical for effective invasive species management, and that globally connected data infrastructures can help countries achieve the goals of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.

Event title: GBIF Gap Finder: Turning National Biodiversity Data Gaps into Action
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: Veronika.Johansson@nrm.se; Kevin.Holston@nrm.se; Manash.Shah@nrm.se; Swedish Museum of Natural History
Event description:
We cannot protect what we cannot see. Even in a data-rich country like Sweden, knowledge of nature has blind spots. The GBIF Gap Finder, developed by GBIF Sweden within the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) network, tries to make those gaps visible.
We developed an open-source pipeline in the programming language R (https://github.com/GBIF-Sweden/gbif_gap_finder): a step-by-step recipe any country can adapt to assess what data is missing from GBIF at a national scale. It reveals gaps at taxonomic (which species groups are under-recorded), spatial (which areas are under-surveyed) and temporal (where recent records are lacking) levels. Its interactive dashboard opens with a plain-language summary.
This live demonstration focuses on Sweden, walking through the different tabs and highlighting the findings that lead to a clear priority list for future data mobilization plans.
Objective: to show how GBIF national nodes and partners can use the tool to steer data mobilization (where to survey, what to digitize, whom to involve), supporting Target 21 of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Key messages:
- An open, reusable tool that lets every country map its own gaps.
- Finding gaps can help prioritize where to act and mobilize data next.

Event title: Advancing Indicator 22.1 on Land Tenure and Land Use through National Partnerships
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance

Event description: This session presents progress on CBD headline indicator 22.1 — the traditional knowledge indicator on land tenure and land-use change in the traditional territories of Indigenous Peoples and local communities — one year after its adoption as a headline indicator. Convened by the technical working group supporting the indicator's development (including custodian FAO, ILC and partners), the session reviews how Parties are engaging with the indicator through their Seventh National Reports (7NRs), and shares early lessons from an emerging cohort of countries — including Kenya, Colombia and the Philippines, among others — that are pioneering whole-of-society approaches to build the data, partnerships and institutional processes needed to report on it. Panelists will discuss practical experience generating and validating land tenure and land-use data together with Indigenous Peoples' organizations, local communities and government agencies; the opportunities and challenges of applying the indicator nationally; and what these early experiences mean for other Parties preparing to report in future cycles. The session aims to connect national practitioners, CBD negotiators and the broader biodiversity data community around a shared, replicable pathway from headline indicator to national implementation.

Event title: All-Ireland Pollinator Plan – empowering people through biodiversity data
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
Submitted timing preference: Flexible - any timeslot on 26th to 28th October
List any other organizations, collaborat: GBIF
Event description: Established in 2015, the All-Ireland Pollinator Plan is a voluntary initiative that has empowered people to come together to tackle biodiversity loss. It works by clearly explaining what wild pollinators need, and what simple, evidence-based actions everyone across society can take to help. Sectoral resources for farmers, local authorities, businesses, communities, and others are freely available at [pollinators.ie]pollinators.ie. Currently the Plan is supported by all 42 local council's in Ireland and more than 400 businesses.  The All-Ireland Pollinator Plan is built on data. It uses species data to understand the status of pollinators; and monitoring data to track changes and the impact of the evidence-based actions. A publicly accessible GIS-based data capture system maps individual actions. Already over 15,000 actions have been logged, helping to connect individuals and transform how local areas are managed for nature. The 2026-2030 Plan is supported by 130 organisations and will help deliver the Nature Restoration Regulation targets in Ireland. Based on the distance a solitary bee will fly to find food, it has an ambitious target of pockets of nature every 200 metres in our landscape, providing food, shelter, and safety for pollinators. It aims to bring about an island that supports biodiversity, is climate resilient, and is a place where we can all experience the health benefits of connecting with nature.

Event title: Strengthening national species services and interoperable biodiversity data systems for GBF monitoring and reporting
Paired thematic focus: From Data to Decisions + Data Gaps & Governance
List any other organizations, collaborat: Catalogue of Life, SANBI, CBD
Event description:
This side-event will showcase how the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF), working with the Catalogue of Life (COL), South African National Biodiversity Institute (SANBI) and partners, supports Parties through interoperable national checklists, hosted portals and shared biodiversity data infrastructure. These services enable countries to align national taxonomic concepts with globally harmonized biodiversity data while retaining national relevance and terminology.
The Catalogue of Life provides the most consistent and up-to-date global checklist of known species and underpins GBIF’s biodiversity occurrence record indexing and interpretation. Through jointly developed tools and infrastructure, countries can build, manage and harmonize national species lists; integrate species names used in national legislation; and improve the quality, usability and interoperability of biodiversity data used in NBSAPs, national reports and GBF indicators, particularly those related to invasive alien species, threatened species and biodiversity knowledge

Event title: Adopting a right-holders’ responsive approach to biodiversity data collection, monitoring and reporting: discussion with data providers and the African and Asian Subregional Technical and Scientific Support Centres.
Paired thematic focus: Monitoring, Technology & Innovation + Connecting Knowledge Systems & People
List any other organizations, collaborat: CBD Women's Caucus, GBIF, ICCA Consortium, SANBI TSCC, ACB TSCC, CO-OP4CBD
Event description:
Achieving the objectives of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (KMGBF) requires biodiversity data systems that are scientifically robust, interoperable, inclusive, and locally grounded (in line with Targets 21 and 23). In this context, Subregional Technical and Scientific Support Centres (TSCCs) can play a strategic role in facilitating multi-stakeholder engagement and connecting governments, scientific institutions, Indigenous Peoples and local communities, women, and youth. 
On one hand, as knowledge holders, rights holders generate valuable observations, experiences, and analyses on ecosystems and sustainable use, yet these remain insufficiently considered and used in the KMGBF monitoring framework. On the other hand, global and national infrastructures such as the Global Biodiversity Information Facility (GBIF) provide essential mechanisms to mobilise, standardise, and make biodiversity data accessible. Bridging these systems requires respectful, equitable, and effective mechanisms for knowledge exchange and data integration.
The side event will bring together rights-holder-responsive and community-based data platforms, notably the ICCA Registry and the CBD Women’s Caucus, the GBIF as representative of a global data infrastructure, with Asian and African TSCCs. It will explore how TSCCs and data providers can work together with locally-grounded initiatives, strengthen knowledge exchange across governments, scientific institutions, and knowledge holders, contributing to a more inclusive and context-responsive KMGBF monitoring and reporting.
